Wsatql. RELICS. I spray of oak-leaves and some wititered flowers, Gathered by hands that loved to cling to mine; Poor relies of the joys that once were ours, - The days of shade and shine ! I touch the leaves, and hear your voice again, Telling the old sweet story o'er and o'er, '4 Tin I forget the doubt—the change—the pain— The sorrow strange and sore. The past revives, I dream our early dream Of Alpine blossoms on a fragrant sod, Of far, white glories, where the snow-peaks gleam, -1 • And lift our souls to God. , On some lone chalet by a deep blue lake, Where life is full of simple, calm delights, And we might watch the rosy morning break Across the solemn heights. The visions fade ;—the hopes that gave them rise - Have perished, and the love has had its day; My path lies lonely beneath English skies, And yours is far away. - . Yet I press onward, though the way be dim, And thorns spring up where roses used to blow; Through dawn and darkness I will follow Him Who called me long ago. He bade me leave the things I love the best; :4 I held them back from Ills entreating hand, He offered peace; I chose my own unrest, And would not understand. And still His patience never knew decay, And still he waited for the certain end; 4 'There came a storm that swept my joys away, And then I knew my Friend. Fltnew Him by the crown of cruel thorn That sinfullands had woven for His head, And by His promise—" Blest are they that mourn; • They shall be comforted." .And finding One in whom my soul can trust, I turn my face from dreams that proved untrue, 'Leaving old relics crumbling in the dust; For Christ makes all things new.
Therefore your voice has lost the charm of old, .You cannot bind me with a broken spell; The song is ended, and the tale is told, And thus I say—farewell. -..--Good Words. SARAH DOI7D2PSY.

Life is but a short day; but it is a working. iday. He who rejoices over another's fall, rejoices n the devil's victory. The most expensive luxuries are not always the most pleasant. One said that a tavern was a place where madness was sold by the bottle. The surest sign of wisdom is charity; and the best charity is that which never ostensibly parades itself as a charity. Two hogsheads make a butt, but it is not every , asturalist who knows that it takes only one goat's head to do it. Professor: "Name an oxide." Student: "Leather." Professor; "Oxide of what ?" Student: "Oxide of beef." The professor subsided. ,A bright little girl who saw three sisters with hair of tich auburn remarked to her mother. "Seems to me, mamma, that kind of hair must be redheaditary in that family." A Londoner keeps a cow in his backyard, and up to date one hundred and fifty-two milkmen have been no- ticed peeping over the back fence to see what the animal

ooks like. A little fellow went to a blacksmith's to see his father's horse shod., and was watching closely the work of the shoeing. The blactsmith began to Dare the borse's hoof, and thinking this was wrong, the little boy aaid earnestly. "My pa don't want his horse made any smaller." A paper in speaking of a 'beautiful lady of large pro- portions should have said, "Mrs. Smith possessed a form that Juno might envy." The editor went home and left a subordinate to get out the paper. and the next morn- ito• he reed that "Mrs. &rah possessed a form that Jumbo might envy." Boy takes a free ride on the back of a Paddington 'bus. To him the conductor: "Off ye go,' ye young rascal, or I'll knock the inside out of 7e?' Boy, not attempting to get down, replies with dignity : "Now then, sir, be care- ful, I know where to report you in case of incivility to passengers." A countryman sowing "his ground, and two young fellows riding that was, one of them called to him, with an insolent air—" Well, honest fellow," said he, "it is your business to sow, but we reap the fruits of your libour." To which the countryman replied—" It is very likely you may, for I am sowing hemp." "Mother, Where's Bill?" "My son, do not let me hear you say Bill again. You should say William." Well, mother, where s William ?" "in the yard feeding the ducks." "Oh, yes, I see him now. But, mother, what makes the ducks have such broad Williams?" "Go ant to your brother directly, you little scamp, or I will box your ears." Two STORMS OF JENNY Ltxn.—There is a pretty story told of the childhood of Jenny Sind, the famous Swedish singer. She was an orphan, and condemned to live with an ill-tempered old woman in Stockholm, who kept the child busy making hair-plaits. The old lady would carry' them to market to sell, leavingjenny locked in the house till her return. Of course this was forlorn enough for the child, and many a time she cried from loneliness. But one day, in the midst of her tears, she noticed the cat on the floor, who seemed quite as neglected as herself. Taking pussy in her lap. Jeany nursed and comforted her, and went back to her plaiting with a lighter heart. As she sa by the open window she began to sing, and , ber beautiful voice attracted the attention of a lady, who etopped her carriage that she might listen. The neigh- bours told her about poor Jenmy, and the lady took her away from her unhappy surroundings, placed her at /school, and she became, in time, the most celebrated singer of her day.—Here is another story of her later . days :—One morning after she had given a charity eon- -cert, a clergyman found her counting and sealing up the money received, preparatory to distributing it among the poor. He began to compliment her, but she cut him short by saying," It is the only return I can make unto, the good Lord for the gift Ile has bestowed upon me, -which is the great joy of my life. I can only repay Him through the poor and the suffering. This I delight to ,40." Her motive in visiting America was to earn £36,000, , to be used fer educating the poor children of Stockholm, • whose great ignorance and degradation touched her ..sympathetic heart. Just before embarking she remarked '-to a friend," May I not hope for God's blessing upon this work, undertaken for the lambs of Christ's ft ick? My .daily prayer is that I may be spared three years, in order 1..0 carry out my plans for my poor children in Stock- holm.' And what a beautiful tribute was paid to her -character by the father of the late Dean Stanley in say- ' " "never converse with her without feeling myself better man."—Young England. PAIILIAMF.UTAST SLANG.—To "rush a bill" is an ex-

pcession well known in the American Senate. and occa- .sionally also used here. To "hang up a bill" is to pass it through one or more of its stages and then to lay it =side and defer its further consideration for a moreor less

indefinite periad. "Lobbying" is a process familiar to maembers. "Log-coiling" is a somewhat rare term in England, but is well understood at Washington. When backwoodsman ents down a tree his neighbours help him to roll it away, and in return he helps them with their trees; so in Congress, when members support a bill, not because they are interested therein, but simply lo gain the help of its promoters for some scheme of -their own, their actin is called "log-rolling," Another

_ American importation is "bunkum," a word generally used to signify empty, frothy declamation. It is said to be derived horn the action of a speaker who, persisting in talking to an empty house, said he was speaking to Buncombe, the name of the place in North Carolina wliich he represented. The word " platform," when used for the programme of a political party, is often, classed .as an Americanism, but it is really a revival of a use mf the word that was very common in English literature ' h the sixteenth and saventeenth centuries, though less common, perhaps, as a noun than a verb, mean- ing to lay down principles. For instance, Milton, n his •"Reason of Oinirch Government," says hat some "do not this* it for the ease of their incons4quent opinions to grant that Church discipline is platformed in the Bible, but that it is left to tile diaeretion of men." A word that has been a good deal used of late years in connection with politics is " fad." It has hardly yet found its way into the diction- aries; but "fads" are many, sad "faddists" and "fad- mongers" abound. Mr. Sala has suggested that the word is a corruption of " faddle;" to dandle—in French, dorloter. A "faddist" iscontinually dandling and caress- g his "fad." This seems a trifie far-fetched. It is i-lore probably a contraction of " fidfad," a word that has been long in use with much the sa.. e meaning as fad." Edward Moore, writing in-" The World" in 17134, applies the word to a very precise person—" the youngest, who thinks in her lieart tint her sister is no: better than a slattern, runs into the contrary extreme,, she does, an absolute &INA.'" I and Is, in everything From " fidfad" in this sense to the modern "fad" is not st very violent transition. The tendency to abbreviation I s very general. The common Parliamentary word whip" is, of course, a contraction of '`whipper-in." Dickens, in "Sketches by Bo;" tells us haw "Sir Some- body Something, when he was whipper-in for the Go- vernment, brought four men out of their beds to vote n the majority, three of whom died on their way home again." The phrase, the "Massacre of the Innocents," as applied to the abandonment of useful measures at he close of session from lack of time for their discus- -5000, first used by The Times in 1859.--Cornhill alfaaazine.

Subject to the Royal Assent being given to the I Bill now before Parliament, the Ship Canal will ' soon be commenced, providing those who apply and those who have already applied for shares pay the deposit of £2 per share promptly. The short time within which the directors must complete their arrangements, namely, before the 6th of August next, makes it very necessary that all interested in the project should do everything in their power to help the promoters. In the House. of Lords, on Monday, the Duke of Buckingham and Chandos (Chairman of Committee) moved that the order made on the 3rd March last, "That no private bill brought from the House of Commons shall be read a second time after Friday the 24th day of June next," be dispensed with in the case ot the Manchester Ship Canal Bill. He pointed out that the measure dealt solely with financial considerations, and expressed the belief that their Lordships would not hesitate to grant I the exception asked for in his motion. The motion was agreed to, and the bill was read a second time without debate. ThB following is a copy of a circular issued on &thirdly to the applicants for ordinary shares in the Manchester Ship Canal:—" You will receive herewith a formal letter of allotment of ordinary shares conditionally applied for by you, subject to the lerformance of the condition of your applica- tion, and you are advised that it is expected the condition will be performed on or shortly after the Bth inst. At the same time it is necessary that you, should understand that the time at the disposal of the Board is very short, and that the cordial assis- tance of all interested in the company will be necessary for its success. The bill pro- viding for the issue of preference shares has r been passed by the House of Commons, and iwe trust that it will shortly receive the sanction of Parliament, in which event the issue of the preference shares is guaranteed, and , the construction of the canal will be assured, pro- vided the applicants for ordinary shares pay up ..t2 , 1 per share in time to enable the preference shares , to be issued. The preference shares cannot be I issued until .£2 per thare has been paid on the ordinary shares. A special account has been opened opened in our names with the National Provincial Bank of England, Manchester, and we shall be obliged if you will at once pay into account the sum of .C--, being £2 per share on the shares conditionally applied for by you on the following terms, namely :—That as soon as the condi- tion of your application is performed, we have your authority to transfer the amount to the credit of the company in payment of the amount payable in respect of the shares allotted to you as above, but that if the condition opt your application be not performed, the slim so I paid by you shall be returned to you without deduc- tion. Having regard to the urgency of the case, we I ask you to make such payment on or before the 9th IJuly, and the bankers will give you a receipt, on air behalf, on the terms above mentioned.—We are, &C., EGERTON OF TATTON, Chairman; JOSEPH C. LEE, Deputy-Chairman." The condition mentioned in this circular is this :—All applications for ordin- ary shares were made subject to the company bay- ing, before the 6th August, accepted applictytions for ' five millions of share capital in addition to the moneys raised for the purchase of the Bridgwater and the Mersey and Irwell Navigation, this being , specified in the Act of 1885. Part of this five millions is now to come for preference shares, but Parlia- ment has imposed the condition that these shares 1 shall not be issued until .C 2 per share is paid on the I ordinary shares. , The Select Committee of the House of Lords to , examine the Manchester Ship canal Bill will con- sist of the Earl of Kimberley (chairman), Earl Beau- ' i champ, Lord Balfour of Burleigh, Lord Acton, and jLord llenley. ,

The view obtained from the historic spot I left quite an impression that Runcorn, with its present "legal and local clouds" hanging over it, still retains much of the beautiful. in nature to ele- vate and charm. Runcorn Hill, which is formed of keuper sandstone, and which has been quarried Mr centuries, was next visited. Here the members were joined by Mr. Guest, who very kindly explained many interesting details. The magni- ficent section and the various colours of the keuper sandstone made ono of the finest sections ever seen by the members, and was greatly admired. A rough bit of walking brought the members to Messrs. Brundritt and Co's..quarry, the firm having deputed two representatives to conduct the mem- bers through the quarry, and these gentlemen very ably explained matter of interest. In this quarry it was observed that the Frodsham beds, or what is locally called fay, is missing, but again appears in Messrs. Handley's and Mr. Bank's quarries. It was very interesting to note hoW even-bedded and free from dip the strata lies in each of the respective quarries. Returning through Weston village and Weston-road, a halt was made near the residence of Mr. T. Banks, to examine the same fault again, which is so plainly seen in the railway cutting, Norman-road. Retracing their steps across the fields, the members not deeming it advisable to cross the common within range of our volunteer crack shots, the waterworks buildings were admired in passing, and, under shelter of the butts the extreme easterly section of keuper sandstone in Runcorn Hill was viewed. In,the Lowlands-road the last section of sandstone with its filled up fissures was noticed, and the members now being at the station returned to Liverpool by train, having had a most enjoyable and interesting out.

THE QUEEN AND THE IMPERIAT, ItrsTrretrn.—The Queen on Monday laid the foundation-stone of the Imperial Insti- tute at :south Kensington. The ceremony was attended by a large and distinguished assemblage, including all the membe, of the Royal family, the Indian Princes, the fm. eign royalties, English Ministers, judges, military and naval representatives, and delegations from the I.arned so- cietiec. In the address which the Prince of Wales, who is President of the Institute, read to the Queen, the hope was expressed that the institution may promote the commercial and industrial prosperity of all parts of tier Majesty's do- minions, and that the scientific and technical educatitn which the requirements of modern indus:ry render necessary may through its means receive fresh development In reply, the Queen said she would recognise the Imperial In- stitute as a record of the progress made and the splendid results that had been achieved during the fifty years of her reign and as the outcome of the Great Exhibition of 1851. She recognised also that the aims and purposes of the Insti- tute were the advancement 01 the arts and sciences and the development of technic,tl education, which would be of such incalculable benefit te the people of this , country. IN con- clusion, she expressed the hope that the fullest possible benefit would attend the labours in which the Committee have been engaged. An Ode written by Mr. Lewis Morris was sang to music, composed by Sir. A. Sullivan, and the ceremony was brought to a Close. The Queen visited the Albert Hall and presented some prizes to children wbo had written essays on kindness to animals. liar Majesty then returned toWindser.

The Clerk submitted replies be had received from the overseers res- pseting the amount of bonds of the assistant-overseers, and aftr.someconsideration it was resolved that the cletk•com- monteate with guarantee societies as to the terms on which they would gwrantee the fidelity of all the accounting officers of the Union to the extent of £lO,OOO in the aggre- gate, and that he request the Local Government Board to intimate their opinion as to the propriety of the Guardians paying the prey/I%ms. THE WORKHOUSE ALTKRATIONS.—Tbe Clerk read a corn- dtunication from the Local Government Board enclosing copies of an order authorising the Guardians to erect a bakehouse and drying•room at the Workhouse at a cost ot £6OO, and also to borrow the amount named. THE EMIGRATION OF CHILD/Mr.—A letter was read from the Liverpool Catholic Childrene' Protection Society stating that the committee were arranging for the despatch of another party of children under charge of their matron, Mrs Lacy, and wishing to know if the Guardians were disposed to send out any children under those auspices.—Saversl members pointed out that some time ago the Guardians sent out several children to Canada, but as they did not re- ceive satisfactory information about their placing out, it was decided to take no action in the Matter. THE WORKHOUSE BOILERS.--A lettecy/as read from the Boilers Insurance and Steam Power Co., Manchester, stating that on the 23rd ult. they had examined the Workhouse boilers, etc., and found them to be in a good coudition. -

When Hyacinth returned Mine, she found there Tracy Mansfield and his sister, who had walked over from Drumabog, and hearing she was out were waiting ' for her. Tracy came out to meet her, and lifted her ; from her pony, asking her where she had been. I
"To Clanmorris," said she, "and , to some of the cottages. You have heard about Dolan and Creagh,.l Tracy." " Aye ; who has not Doolan is not a man to stick at trifles."

"None of them will, I think, Tracy. Besides, any one of them must do what the Secret Society orders. It is as bad as the Vehmgericht, isn't it?" She'went on into the sitting-room, and Mrs. Desmond looked up smiling from her work. Nelly danced towards her cousin. I _

"Well," she cried, "anything new—been flirting with that handsome Vincent Lorraine again?" Hyacinth flushed crimson. "Don't be silly: Aileen. I have been to Clanmonis, and they are going to give a ball—on the —th." Nellie clapped her bands, and uttered a joyful cry. There was a quick flash of pleasure in Tracy's eyes, though a frown followed it.

Mrs. Desmond asked— "And did they want you to go, Hyacinth?" "Both of us, mother dear. 'You will say yes ?" "It would not be easy to refuse, dear, as they are such old friends, and Terry, too, will be coming home; but I confess I &ill care about meeting Vincent Lorraine, who, of course, will be there." "They have asked him—they told me so," said Hyacinth, for the first time in her life practising casuistry. - • "And bd sure he will accept, if he thinks you will be there," whispered Nellie, in the stage aside. "Don't be so silly Nell," said her brother, quite sharply, while Hyacinth , turned 'away impatiently. She was not wont to mind a jet; but just now every nerve was strung up to an unnatural tension, and Nellie's harmless words were like a stab to her.. Nellie drew back. "I meant no harm," she said; "sure, a , joke will hurt nobody." ' "Never mind," said Mrs. Desmond, laughing, "no bones are broken, my dear." But she glanced at her, young daughter, and wished again that she could avoid, this ball. At the same time she was anxious to see Lorraine, and to judge for herself whether his bearing towards Hyacinth was consistent with the ordinary courtesies of a young man to a beautiful and attractive girl. She had no intention, she said to herself, of per- mitting an idle rout to amuse herself at her child's ex- pense; nor would she have tolerated any serious qatentions from such a man. She did not court rank or .wealth for Hyacinth, and if she had known what had passed between Lorraine and the girl that morning, she Would have, under some excuse or other, declined Mrs. O'Conor's invitation.
Tracy caught Hyacinth's hand, and drew her towards. him.
" Mind," he said, "yon keep some dance's for "Oh, Tracy, of course, but not tOo many, you know —one cannot do that." "Four. Hyacinth." _ _ _ _ _

But Hyacinth shook her head, and would only pro- mise‘three. " I can't give away all the dances before- hand," she said. ." Come, Hyacinth, I am the first who has asked you l" "You won't be the last," retorted the girl, quickly, drawing her hand from his, as if she felt that somehow he must know whose clasp had enclosed it, whose lips kissed it, and hear that soft, but masterful, "You will promise," that rang in her ears. • Tracy looked at her curiously, wondering, with a , fierce pang of jealousy, whether in her own mind she alluded to Vincent Lorraine ; but Hyacinth went up to her mother, and knelt down by her, and said • coaxingly— " And you'll have a new dress, mother dear, won't von?" _ . _
Mrs. Desmond looked down into the deep, pathetic .eyes uplifted her, and involuntarily drew the slight form closer to her. _ .

"No, mavourneen," said she, stroking the clustering curls; "if anything new is bought it will be for you. The satin I wore last year is good &lough for this.' "I need nothing new," said Hyacinth, promptly. "Mrs. O'Conor will have to put up with the &tin and ivy leaves again. Nellie, mind you look very, very grand—you know why." "Too bad ! " said Nellie, col,sering in her turn; " if' you may tease me, I ma F . e you; but then you would fascinate a certain per . l,owever you dressed yourself. You had only the serge' you're wearing now when he first saw you." "Hash! hush !" said gentle Mrs. Desmond, "you had better talk about ball dresses, if you want ;to talk nonsense." _ _

"And you had better come for a walk than do either," said Tracy. "Will you come, Hyacinth?" "Not now, Tracy dear; but I'll go for a long walk to-morrow, if you'll come for me." "Be sure I will," said Mansfield. "Come, Aileen," and brother and sister took their leave.

' Hyacinth," said Mrs. Desmond, when the two were alone again, "I don't want to ask impossibilities of you, but I would like you to avoid Vineent Lorraine as much as you can at this ball. It isn't that I distrust You, ~dear,"-N-Hyacinth's head was drooping and her face hidden from her inother —" but you are very . . - .
young, and not used to men such u he-is. If,l ha-cl been in Mrs O'Conor's place I should not have asked . .
him at all. I think men who lead reckless and wicked lives oncht not to be countenanced:. but I am afraid

Mrs. O'Oonor has same hopes for norine. The idea that a 'reformed rake makes a good husband' is a ter- ribly false one. I don't suppose Lorraine Means to do more than amuse himself, and that is bad enough, if he were not the gambler and rout he is."
"I shall avoid him as much es I can, mother dear, yon may be sure," said the girl. "I don't like him," And then she talked of something else. •

But that night, lying awake, sbe could not help, angry though she still was with Lorraine, wondering if he would have been different if his mother had lived. She had dietl, the girl knew, when he was quite in in- fant, and some of the tenants, who had seen her once or twice, said she was a " swate lady." There must be good in a. man who could love as he could—when he . .
c-hose. Had she not seen some glimpses of that good?

How tender he was to Biddy, although he professed not to like children! and under his cynical philosophy lay more feeling for the sick child than he cared to oWn ; or, perhaps, he was hardly aware of its existence. Then the girl's thoughts went to her promise. Ought she to have told her mother of that? But how could she?
She did not know.ho'w or why she gave it; .he. did not
•c
I) ti

wish to do it, yet it was given, and -she must fulfil. it ; at any rate, she did not want to break it—that would make Lorraine think she was afraid of him. No, she would be silent; but it troubled her that she should have kept anything from her mother. Poor • child ! would it have been better for her in the end if she had told all? The' next day Tracy and Hyacinth, in the course of their walk, met Farmer, Grady,.who reported Biddy still very ill, but the doctor thonght not dangeronsly ill. Mr. Lorraine, the farmer added, had left Curra- more—not for good,--ocb, never fear; that would be welcome news. No, he had ten that morning; nobody knew for what place or what length of time. But perhaps, Grady saki with a sneer, be was gone to.make sure of constabuley to help him when the day came. for birning out his tenants. Whatever his errand and his destination, Mr. Lor- raine did, not return to Curramore till within three days of the ball; and, meanwhile, grand preparations were going forward in "many an ancient hall" round- about, and the ,two' flys that 'Trahone boasted were bespoken to perfonn prodigies in the way of carrying guests; and Terence O'Conor had come home from the Curragh, and the very same day rode over to the Wood ,Cottage. though, to be sure, he had first seen pretty Nellie Mansfield. A fine, open-brewed, hand- some young fellow was Terence, and when Hyacinth, with a glad cry, sprang to meet him, he held both her hands, and jaid merrily— "Faith, ye grow more beautiful, dear, every time I see you; but Irm half afraid to kiss you now, though I should like to, very much." , • "Oh, you are like my own brother. Terry," the girl answered, with happy laughter, and Terence needed no further hint.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TIIESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at 4 p.m. QUESTIONS AND NOTICES.

In reply to Mr. Johnson, Lord G. Ilmatxrow said it was true that on Sunday, the 19th June, the officer in com- mand of her Majesty's gunboat Rupert allowed a party of Roman Catholic officers and men to attend, under arms, a service held in St. Charles's Roman Catholic Church, Hull, in celebration of her Majesty's Jubilee. Being under arms, the sailors, as was usual in such a cue, presented arms at the consecration and elevation of the Edcharist. The Admiralty were not consulted in the matter, and his opinion was that, except under very exceptional circumstances, sailors should not be allowed to carry arms when attending divine service. Sir Juan FREGUSSON said, in reply to Sir E. Birkbeck, that the portion of the negotiations in reference to a convention for the prohibition of "floating grog-shops" in the North Sea was this :—Her Majesty's Government were awaiting the reply of the Netherlands Government (which might shortly be expected) with respect to certain amendments of the proposed convention which had been suggested by Germany, and assented to by England. In answer to Mr. Howell, Mr. H. MATTHEWS said that the letter dated Windsor Castle, 22nd June, 1887, and signed by her Majesty with the initial of her Indian title, was addressed to the subscribers to the Women's Jubilee Fund, amongst whom were women, both European and native, who had contributed sums amounting to £l,OOO from Ceylon, and £l,OOO from Burmah.—Mr. CONY* Buns remarked that the letter was addressed to the women of Great Britain and Ireland, and Mr. Howut, Intimated his intention to call attention to the subject on a future cccasion. . _ .

--Mr. G. Howsta. subsequently gave notice for the first opportunity to call attention to the use, in the United Kingdom, of her Majesty's Indian title of Empress, and to move that in the opinion of the House the title of Empress in papers and documents in the United King- dom, other than those appertaining to her Indian posses- sions, is contrary to the express pledges given in Parliament when the title was conferred, and should be discontinued. (Hear, hear.) Mr. CAtIPBELL-BANNERMAN gave the following notice of amendment to the motion for the second reading of the Land Bill (Ireland) : "That the House, taking Into view the circumstances set forth in the report of the Royal Commission of 1886 on the Land Acts of 1881 and 1885, and the recommendations of the Commission, is of opinion that no bill for the amending of the. law relating to land tenure in Ireland can be deemed satisfactory that does not provide not only for the entitling of lease- holders to the benefit of the Act of 1881, but also for af- fording such means for the revision of judicial rents fixed under the act as would meet the exigencies created by the heavy fall in agricultural prices since the passing of that act." Sir JAMES FERGUSSOV said, in reply to Mr. Bryce, that SS far as her Majesty's Government. are informed the Turkish Convention had not been ratified by the Sultan. Of course. if the. Convention should lapse, there would be no subsidiary agreement, and in no event would there be any note altering the sense of the principal instru- ment or imposing any obligation upon this country. Although the extended period for ratification has ex- pired, her Majesty's Government. are very desirous of fulfilling their intentions towards the Stilt Jti and the Powers. and would not refuse to accept the ratification were it. to be tendered before the departure of her 3,iajesty's special Commissioner, which in any ease will Nice place within a few days. Tie was instructed to leave in the course of the present week. TIIE CASE OF MISS CASS.
TIM GOVERNMENT DEFEATED OA MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT.

In reply to Mr. Atherley Jones, Mr. Johnston, and Mr. Chamberlain, Mr. H. MATTTIEWS declined to institute an inquisitorial inquiry into the character and conduct of Miss Cass, the lady who had been arrested by a police- constable on a charge of misconduct. He stated that she had her legal remedy if she thought herself aggrieved by the conduct of the police in arresting her. Up to an hour before he came down, to the House, TiO complaint had been lodged against the police. If such a complaint were made, the Chief Commissioner would no doubt either inquire into it himself, or, if it amounted to a criminal charge, would send it for investigation to a police magistrate. It appeared to him (Mr. Matthews) that the charge which seemed to be made, against the policeman was one of perjury, and it would therefore be wrong in him to express any opinion upon it, or to say more than that every facility would be given for an inquiry into it. Ile could not undertake to institute any inquiry ink) the conduct of the magistrate in the case (Mr. Newton), who held an office entirely independent of him, or of any other member of the Lxecutive Government.

Subsequently Mr. ATTIERLEY JONES, having obtained leave, by forty members rising in their places, moved the adjournment of the House in order to discuss a question of urgent public importance, namely, the case of Miss Cass. That young lady, he said, arrived in Lon- don six weeks ago, and had always borne an irreproach- able character. She obtained employment, under a Mr. Bowman, in Southampton-row, Holborn. One night last week she went to Jay's, in Regent-street, to buy some gloves, and found the shop shut. She was then arrested by a police constable on a charge of soliciting,- and brought before Mr. Newton, police magistrate at, Marl- borough-street, who, refusing to accept the statement of Mrs. Bowman as to the girl's irreproachable dharacter, asserted his belief that she had gone nut for immoral purposes. Thereupon tbe girl was discharged with a caution not to walk in Regent-street at night in future. Surely if the case was one in , which the magi- strate thought it right to charge the accused, he had no right, after the denial made by her and her employed, and on the unconfirmed testimony of a police constable. to send the young woman away with the brand he had put upon her. (Cheers.) In conclusion, the hon. and learned member urged that it was the duty of the Home 'Secretary to insist on an inquiry into the case and the conduct and antecedents of the police constable. Mr. DODDS, who seconded the motion, bore testimony to the good character borne by Miss Cass before she 'came to'Londan, he being acquainted with her father, and knowing that all the members of his family were regarded as among the most respectable and well- behaved people in Stockton. The DOME SECRETARY admitted that the hon, gentle- men who had brought the case forward were justified in what they had done by their' belief that an almost irre- parable injury had been done to Miss •Case, but, pointed out that he had no power to institute a, thorough inquiry into the matter. He knew that lie could order an inquiry by the police officials, but that would be one of the most unsatisfactory nature. It, was evident frotn the evidence of the police constable that his statement was either true or false, and any inquiry into the case must involve the inquiry as to whether he had committed perjury with no power to examine witnesses on oath, or to have the investigation conducted by means of advocates, and with the examination of witnesses he did not, see how it was possible for him in a case involving the crimival charge of perjury to order an inquiry. The young:lady whose conduct had been called in question by the action of the police constable had both a civil and criminal remedy, and it would not be right, for him to prejudice either course by eccpressing premature opinions in that House. Mr. J. CHAMBERLAIN reminded the House that the Home Secretary had premised an inquiry if a prima facie case were made out, and went on to contend that a prima facie case had already been established. The right hon. gentleman proceeded to comment on the con- duct of the chief magistrate, and expressed the opinion that Mr. Newton ought to be called upon in his own in- terest to explain the course he had tal:en.—The ATTORNEY-GENERAL suggested that its it'was impossible toturn the House into a Court of appeal on this question the proper course would be that those who had taken up the cause should submit the statements of the parties in .writing,to the authorities and leave to them the respon- sibility of deciding whether a prosecution should or should not he instituted for perjury. Mr. CAINE, in supporting the motion, accused the police of the Metropolis of being in the habit of levying black- mail from tvomen in the streets, and argued that this was the root of the evil disclosed in the present case. Mr. CHILDERS assumed that the case would be for- mally stated in writing, so that the suggestion of the Attorney-General could he carried out. It might be that on the judicial investigation matters would come out that would cause the Home Secretary to communicate with the Lord Chancellor in reference to the condudt of the police magistrate. - After some remarks from Sir R. Fowler, Mr. Jacob Bright, and Mr..H.,H. Fowler, the last of whom ,asked for a distinct pledge from the Government that there should be an inquiry; into this case Mr. W. H. Siiirrn urgell that it was not reasonable to ask for such a pledge after the promise already made on behalf of the Government. A ate the magistrate admitting that it might be right to demand an -explanation from him, the right hon. gentleman contended that it would not be right to ask for that, explanation until the pre- vious proceeding had been taken. With regard to the allegations made by Mr. Caine as to the conduct of the police generally, lie hoped tile hen. gentleman would make those allegations in a specific form, so that they might be duly inquired into. (Hear, hear). Alter some remarks by Mr. Pickergill, Lord R. Mr. L. BRIGHT asked the Rome Secretary whether hie authorities had any record of black-mailing on the part of the police of the metropolis ; and whether on certain occa- sions it had been found necessary to rtniove police con- stables in considerable number from the West End to the East End of London, where the opportunities for the prac- tice were less frequent Mr. MATTREws : The notice given of this question has been too short for full information to ba furnished. I have just seen the Chief Commissioner. who informs me that since he has been in office there has been no case sr black- mail recorded. I will make inquiry. If the hon. member will be good enough to repeat nis question .an accurate answer will be furnished. . .

Mr. L. BRIGHT said he would put the question again to- morrow. Mr. W. H. Satrrse—l think it will be for the convenience of the House that I should state the course which the Gov- ernment have thought it right to take under all the cir- cumstences of the division which took place yesterday. The Government are under the impression that the House acted under some misconception—(a laugh)—last evening. There is no doubt whatever that it is the duty of the Gov- ernment to institute an inquiry into the circumstances at the case—(Ministerial cheers)—and to see that the inquiry shill be full and complete. (Hear, hear.) The Lord Chancellor will call on Mr. Newton for an explanation of the proceedings in the case which formed the subject of de- bate last evening witheut any delay—(hear, hear)—and such further steps will be taken as will secure a cemplete and impartial inquiry into all the circumstances. (Cheers.) It will be satisfactory to the House that I should make this statement, as an assurance that the Government feel no less than any member of this House the absolute importance —(Opposition, laughter, and Ministerial cheers)—of se- curing that the characters of persons who are accused shall be protected as much as it is possible to protect them, and that the police of the metropolis, on whom so much de- pends far the good order and security of this great city, shall also be placed under circumstances which will se- cure as far as possible the complete rectitude' of their pro- ceedings under all conditions and at all times. (Hear, hear.) Mr. H. FOWLER :—ln order that there may be no miscon- ception as to the course the Government intend to pursue, I wish to ask whether we are to understand that the Govern- ment do not propose that this inquiry should be conducted by the director of public prosecutions, with a view to seeing whether an indictment for perjury can be sustained. (Hear, bear.) That, I understand, was the distinct issue on which the House voted last night. Do I understand that what the right bon. gentleman means is, that ,a proper inquiry will be instituted under the direction of the Home Secretary, as the head of the metropolitan police, with reference to the conduct of the policeman in this case? I understand, of course, that the Lord Chancellor will deal with the magis- trate, but what wadisitint to iequire into is the conduct of the policeman. ( r, hear.) Mr. W. H. SMITH: The course the Government think it most advisable to pursue is, that the Lord Chancellor shall call on the magistrate to give an explanation of all the pro- ceedings in this case, and that when the Lord Chancellcir has received that explanation such further steps shall be taken as will secure a full and impartial inquiry into the circumstances. Whether that course should be an inquiry conducted by the Secretary of State or an inquiry taking the oharacter of a proeecution must depend on such explanations as w,e receive, but there will be no delay, and no efforts will be left untried to make that inquiry impartial and com- plete. (Hear, hear.) The right bon, gentleman asks that I should undertake that there shall he an indictment for perjury. , Mr. H. FOWLER :No ; I want to know whether there will be an inquiry by the director of public prosecutions, in order to see whether he thinks there should be an indict- ment for perjury. Mr. W. H. SMITH : We shall act on our responsibility, and in a manner which we think most likely to secure the most absolutely impartial inquiry into all the circum- stances of the case ; but. we must retain our discretion as , to the particular method lay which we should proceed, until we have more information on the subject than we possses af• present. Mr. herernworma asked whether the satisfaction of the publiv demand for an inquiry into the conduct of the police was in some way to hang on the private inquiry to be Instituted by the Lord Chancellor into the proceedings of the magistrate. The House and the country would expect that these two inquiries should be entirely separate— (cheers)—and it would be altogether unsatisfactory if the question concerning the police were to be postponed or shelved pending any other inquiry. (Oppoeition cheers.)

Mr. W. H. SMITH: I must protest agains the suggestion that we wish to postpone or shelve the matter. (Ministerial cheers.) Our object is to arrive at the truth with regard to both parts of this important inquiry. We simply say that we must ascertain what the facts of the Case are, and we will then proceed with regard to the policeman and the magistrate as the ends of justice may seem ta require. I can give no other explanation to the House, but I assure the House that there is not the slightest disposition to delay or shelve the matter. (Ministerial cheers). Mr. DODDS said be deeply regretted that the Government 'did not state to the House yesterday the course they hart now announced. (Cries of 'Order.") However, it would be quite understood. (Renewed (nits of "Order.") . . ..
h e SPEAKER said lie must remind the hon. member tbat there was no question before the House. . .

Mr. DODDS replied that if be were not allowed to address to the House the few words he had to say be should be under the necessity of moving its adjournment again. (Cheers and laughter.) He merely desired to say that no inquiry would be satisfactory to Miss Case and her friends which did not afford her an opportunity of completely vindicating her character as being, as he believed her to be, as innocent a young woman as any in the Metropolis. (Hear, hear.)
Mr. Osmium MORGAN asked whether the form and method of the second inquiry would depend upon the result of the first.

Mr. W.U. SMITH said he had stated that the inquiry shoeld be complete in both parts. Mr. PICKEESGILL asked the First Lord of the Treasury to explain why the inquiry into the conduct of the policeman should not proceed concurrently with the inquiry into the conduct of the magistrate. (Hear, hear.) _

- Mr. W. H. itarrn : I have given an engagement to the House, and I think it should be accepted. (Ministerial cheers.) The inquiry should be made without delay. Mr. Dimote asked whether, as the Government had taken the whole time of the House, they whuld take security agatest such a scandalous waste of time as °mired last night, and whether, with a view to that end, they would in future make their etatements before and not after a division, (Opposition cheers and laughter, and Minis- Aerial cries of "Order.") THE COERCION BILL.

On the motion fo-r-illti-ChTri;Wcini;i-the Crimea Bill, Me. GLADSTONE moved the rejection of the measure. He said the distinction between former Coercion Bills And the present one was broad. The old coercion was aimed at crime; the new Coercion was aimed at association, the only weapon by which the poor could hope to redress the in- equality of their struggle with wealth, power, and adminis- trative authority. There was no justification for the measure, there being no exceptional amount of crime at present in Ireland, and stbere being also less crime there than in this country. Discussing the penalty attaching to combining for exclusive dealing, the right hon. gentleman said there was a good deal of exclu- sive dealing in this country, yet it had not been made a crime. The Government durst not lift a finger in defence of such a proposal for England as was contained in this bill. When the Local Government Bill of his Government was rejected last year, they predicted that it would come to thia—that there was no alternative between a legislative as- sembly for Irish affairs and a sterner form of coercion than the Irish people had ever experienced. Those who then left him—with the exception of Sir George Trevelyan and one or two others—bad made it possible by their support to Pass such a bill as this. Why, he asked, was the state of

thines now existing between England and Ireland so pre- cious and valuable that people should desire to maintain it? No other part of the Queen's dominions was held by force, but Ireland was held by force. He could not understand what the party opposite was fighting for. They seemed to be fighting for something which appeared to be nothing but the hatred of the two countries, the profuse waste of public treasure, the stoppage of our own vital and necessary busi- nesF, and the incurring of the judgment and condemnation of all the civilised world. In the faith that 'these things conld not last, be moved the rejection of the bill.—Mr. BALFOCIR followed the ex-Premier in the debate. He said tbat during the month just ended there had been a relapse from the improvement which was taking place in Ireland, due, he believed, to the inflammatory speeches of Mr.Dayitt. —The debate was adjourned about midnight.
FOREIGN NEWS.
THE EGYPTIAN CONVENTION.

CONSTANTINOPLE, SATORDAY.—The British Government, in reply to the request made by the Porte ;on the 30th ult., has declined to grant a fresh extension of the period for the ratification of the Egyptian Convention, and this decision was communicated to the Ottoman Govern- ment by Sir H. D. Wolff to-day. Another Council of Ministers has consequently been held to consider the matter. _

PARIS, MONDAY NIGHT.—The Constantinople correspon- dent of the Temps says that not only will Austria, Ger- many:, and Italy support England against Franceland Russia in connection with the Egyptian Convention, but that a distinct understanding exists between Italy and England on the subject of any military measures which may be necessary. CONSTANTINOPLE, MONDAY EVENINO.—The Commis- sioners for the Egyptian Convention held a long confer- ence to-day. Sir H. Wolff is proposing to leave in a few days. Mahmoud Pacha, President of the Legislative Sec- tion of the Council of State, has been appointed Commis- sioner for the settlement of the Cretan question, and leaves this evenine for Crete. THE PORTE AND THE EGYPTIAN CONVENTION.

CONSTANTINOPLE, TETESDAY.—Tba Convention has not yet been ratified by the Sultan; but in well-informed quar- ters the belief is now entertained that it will be. WEDNE:DAIL—The instructions received by Sir Drum- mond Wolff from Lord Salisbury refer) solely to the ex- tension of the British Commissioner's stay in the Turkish capital until next Sunday, but do not state that a fresh de- lay has been granted for the ratification. Nevertheless, if the imperial Trade authorising the ratification be rro- mulgated before Sunday next the ratifications will be ex- changed. In the contrary case, however, Sir Drummona Wolff will certainly leave Con•tantinople next Sunday.

MEETING OF THE BULGARIAN SOBRANJE. TIRNOVA, MONDAY.—The Sobranje was opened at half- past one this afternoon. Several new members having been sworn, the House proceeded to the election of President, M. Tontcheff, the candidate proposed by M. Statnbouloff, being chosen by 275 votes against 74 re- corded in favour of M. Vatcheff, and a like number in favour of M. Gueshoff. The Opposition candidate, M. Zachariah Stojanoff, was elected vice-president, and assured the House that as long as lie held the office he would use every effort to keep M. Katkoff and the Prince of Mingrelia away from the country. The Sobranje subse- quently adjourneckuntil to-morrow, when the report of the mission of the Bulgarian delegates to Europe last year will be considered. It is asserted that the Govern- ment has three candidates for the vacant throne.

DEATH OF TUE MARQUIS OF WINCUESTER.—The The death was announced, on Monday, at his residence, Amport, near Andover, of the Marquis of Winchester, who was born June, 1801; and who succeeded to the title in 1843. He is succeeded by his eldest son, Augustus John Henry, Earl of Wiltshire, born in 1858. At Belfast Police-court on Monday Patrick Mc.Mahon‘ ringleader of the mob who attached the police on Sunday in the Central Railway Fields during a party riot, was sentenced to six months' hard labour. Five other rioters, including two women, were sent to gaol for one month, while a boy named O'Hara was ordered to be whipped. The now very rare verdict of .felo de se was returned by a Plymouth jury on Saturday night in the case of a man named Thomas Jolly. Ile had tied his feet and hands together and then thrown himself into the water, having previously announced his intention of com- mitting suicide in that particular way. I MR. GLADSTONE ON THE IRISH) QUESTION: REPLY TO LORD -HARTINGTON. Mr. Gladstone was present o'n Saturday evening at. a . dinner given by Sir Joseph Pease, M.P., to a numteer of Liberal members for north-eastern constituencies. The company drank the health of the eh eters of Spalding.— Replying to the toast of his 'health, the Ex-Painarea made &speech in which were some important references to the Irish' euestion. Without faith and patience, he said, it was, in his opinion, impossible to do justice to great questions in great controversies, because great contro- versies had their alterations and vicissitudes. Those present might perhaps. recollect how dark were some of the years during what was .familiarle known as the time of "Jingoism." But how right wen. those who at that dark period trusted the people, and found when the day of trial came the people heel wen deserved and answered to their trust; and he believed what we then experienced was a principle applicable to every such controversy, and that in the crisis of the present day, which for the three kingdoms was even a greater and more vital crisis than that of ten years ago, faith and patience were more absolutely essential. (Hear, hear.) At the same time he admitted that flesh and blood received a certain satisfaction when faith and patience derived sup- port from external signs., end unquestionably the sign which that day had yielded was of a most remarkable and significant character. If the change of opinion in the case of Spalding, where it was not lass than 14 or 15 per cent, of the numbers polled, was an average change, then if by any accident Parliament were dissolved the elec- tion would result in a complete revolution in the rela- tions of parties. However, they must look patiently and quietly at the fact that they were engaged in a very stiff contest indeed. He proceeded to criticise Lord Harting- ton's recent speeches at Manchester and Blackburn, which, be said, contained a manly, intelligent, and able' setting, forth of the case from Lord Hartington's point of view. The member for Rossendale admitted that we were still in the midst of a crisis of a serious and grave character, and he (Mr. Gladstone) was glad to register that admission, because there had been a disposition among, the Unionist party to proceed on the basis that unless there was a great deal of crime and disturhance in Ireland, nobody need trouble them- selves about the Irish question. We were in the midst of a grave and serious crisis in a double sense. We were trampling under foot the whole wishes and convictions of the Irish people, and Parliament was reduced to para- lysis and impotence. But, although the Irish q,uestion monopolised the attention of Parliament, not a word WAS said in the House of Commons about the liotne Rule controversy, which lay at the root of the Irish question. Then Lord Harlington said that the evictions in some parts of Ireland Were a public scandalo, public disgrace, and a public danger. That language was perfectly satisfactory to him (Mr. Gladstone). But how was this to be dealt with? The state of things which presented itself was that of a tenant who had an interest in his holding, sanctioned and consecrated by the law under the name of tereant-right, and who was threatened with the confiscation of that interest through the rent, which had become excessive. A Royal Commission, con- sisting of men who were known not to entertain violent prejudice against the landlord, recommended that under these circumstances the rents should be judicially recon- sidered; le.' Lord Hartington refused the reeemmendne tion and k. (lor the Land Bill the Irish term.. who had a legal interest in his holding, was to have no relief unless he submitted himself to the degrading condition of bank- ruptcy. Of all things most demoralisine to be preached to a population by a Legislature was that of submission to bankruptcy, 'which was advocated by Lord Hartington as the remedy of' a state of things which he had himself characterised as a condition of public disgrace, scandal, end danger. That was a questimewhich would have to come before Parliament, which wbuld have to say that the tenant should receive no relief unless thrcugh bank- ruptcy. Lord Hartington had been subject to extra- ordinary illusions, and had stated that he was unaware that there was any disagreement about Ireland among friends until a comparatively recent period—about a yeas, ago. He (Mr. Gladstone) would, however, remind him that about April or January, 1886, was not the first period when he was aware of differeaces of opinion, for in the month of September, 1885, Lord Harlington made declarations upon Irish policy which were of such a character that he immeliately addressed a letter of the strongest remonstrance to him. He even went a little further back, and without being able to go into details, which would not be right, he would remind Lord Harlington that four months before September, 1885, the gravest differences ,upon Irish policy had arisen, when he (Lord Hartington) was- on one and he (Mr. Gladstone) on the other side. Furthermore, in the month of February, he believed in 1883—he would not. say absolutely that it was not 1884, though he believed it was 1883—when he was staying at Cannes, when Lord Harlington in a public speech declared that no further extension whatever of local liberties and local institutions could be given to Ireland until the Irish members had entirely repented of their evil ways and had adopted a different cause of politics, he thouget the statement so astounding that at first he would not be- lieve it, but afterwards found it too true. It was there- fore for Lord Harlington to say whether or no at that time le, was not aware of the differences at that time.' The statement was certainly received by himself with little less than horror, and he believed also by the great bulk of those with whom he acted. Unless, therefore, his statements could be shaken he asked them whether Lord Hartington was justified in representing .that he had been in a fool's paradise, and believed that perfect harmonee upon Irish policy had existed among them until little more than a year ago. Lord Harlington again said that to introduce anything like separate insti- tutions that Ulster or a portion of Ulster might roil-0;e, "would require a complete and thorough remodelling of the scheme proposed by the late Government for the government of Irelan.i." Lord Hartington's memory had again played him false, because the direct contrary of what he said was found in the speech which he (Mr. Glad- stone) made on the part of the Government in April, 1886. wherein he distinctly declared that if a practical scheme could be suggested or was -desired by Ulster, they were ready at any moment to entertain it. Lord Hartington further said that if they refused the presence of Irish representatives they would lose the only title by which Parliament bad the right to concern Itself with Irish affairs. But had they any representatives in the House of Commons from the colony of New South Wales, and had they renounced the right to interfere in the affairs of New South Wales? Lord Hartington said that his colleagues had been opposing a Coercion Rill, but that they themselves had on former occasions initiated legis- lation of that character. He (Mr. Gladstone) said that that proposition was untrue. They had initiated legislation of that character in so far as it aimed at the suppression of crime. But there were three essential differences in which all thelegislation with which they had been concerned was at variance with the legislation now unhappily before Par- liament. In the first place, they (the Liberals) had neeer introduced legislation for the purpose of enlarging the criminal law of the country and setting up as crimes what were never known as crimes before. (Hear, hear.) In the second place, they have never given over to an executive officer like Lord Castlereagh, or an Irish Secre- tary like Mr. Balfour, the power of determining the innocence or guilt- of an individual with reference to belonging to particular associations, and of cancelling the right and essentially attached to a British subject of a judicial hearing of his case, and Lord Harting- ton had no right to say that they bad ever counten- anced a principle which from the bottom of their hearts they abominated and detested. (Hear, hear.) Thirdly., he was not aware that they had ever in- troduced a Coercion Bill with that malign stigma of perpetuity stamped upon it. Those three points he placed in contradiction to that gross though unwitting error of Lord Hartington, when he said that his colleagues, for- sooth, previously introduced similar legislation. Lord Har- tington then said that combinations like Trades Unions would not be touched by the present bill. It was true Trades Unions were exempt. They knew the importance of Trades Unions in respect of the social and economical conditions of England, and what the Liberals had con- tended was that the principle of protection afforded to Trades Unions should be extended to the Irish occupier of land; but it was withdrawn from him. They in- tended on Monday night to ask the Government whether they would consent to give to the Irish what they had given 'to the English Trades Unions. He agreed with Lord Hartington that the time was not pro- pitious for conference on the subject of Liberal Union. They had often heard him (Mr. Gladstone) accused of drawing subtle distinctions. (Laughter.) They would excuse him if he now drew a subtJe distinction. In his opinion' while the Liberal party was more divided than ever in the House of Commons, he did not admit it out- side of the House of Commons, as regarded the country, and in support of this he appealed to the elections of Liverpool, Burnley South Derbyshire, and Spalding. They were told that the Liberal party was in two sec- tions. -Where was the second section at Spalding? (Hear, hear.) The fact was that the second section could not permanently exist, not could it exist for any length of time. Gentlemen who cOmposed it would have to choose one course or another. Lord Hartington had proposed that a plan for the government of Ireland should be concocted in a kind of Grand Committee in Parliament. He examined sir detail this suggestion of a Grand Committee for formu- lating a plan of Irish government, and thought it would probably fail in its purpose front the fact that no 'lrish members were proposed to be admitted. Let the principle that Ireland should manage her own affairs be first admitted, and there would be no difficulty in meet- ing to determine the particulars of a scheme under which Ireland should enter upon the enjoyment of her rights. He pointed out that in three particulars Ireland possessed elements of strength which she never possessed before. In the first place, a constituency so extended that it spoke undeniably and with authority and voice of the nation; secondly, a representative body entitled to set forth the judgment and conviction of the coun- try: thirdly, from end to end of Britain a vast' portion of the people enthusiastically enlisted in her cause. These three things were the three strands of the rope, so , strong that there was no hope of those opposed to them i breaking it in pieces. It was a bond which would float the ship of State through all the present controversy into the harbour of security, of bowel; and of repose. (Cheers.) LORD HARTINGTON AND THE UNIVERSITIES. div.head: FRANCE:-RAILWAY ACCIDENT,
div.p: FRANCE:-RAILWAY ACCIDENT,

PAWS, SUNDAY NIGHT.—An accident has occurred at the Orleans terminus, which in other circumstances might have caused fearful loss of life. The new Pyrenees express, with restaurant and luxurious carriages attached. was making its return journey without a single passen- ger. At. Orleans the train ,arrived an hour late. The driver, named Quinet, wishing to make up for lost time, increased the speed to nearly 80 miles an hour, the result being that the slackening at the Paris terminns was in- sufficient, and that the train not only dashed through the buffers, but through a thick wall. The driver, stoker, and guard were badly injured, and three carriages were smashed. The restaurant car was also thrown off the line much damaged. Quinet, the driver, is in a dying state. _ _

- - MADRID, SUNDAY.—In Valencia to-day the populace attacked and destroyed the houses of the collectors of the octroi duties, as a means of protestation against municipal taxes. Military precautions were taken, and several arrests made. According to the latest intelligence from the governor tranquillity has been restored. MADRID, MONDAY.—The agitation at Valencia against the municipal taxes continues. Martial law has been proclaimed, and a number of arrests made. MADRID, MONDAY NIGHT.—The rioting which broke out at Valencia yesterday, in consequence of taxation grievances, was renewed to-day, in spite of the fact that the military had been called out. The crowd, daring almost to madness, fired on the troops, who quickly returned the fire, killing one person and wounding several others. AFGHAN BOUNDARY QUESTION. EX-

ST. PErERSBURO, SUICIDAL—Sir West Ridgeway. on re- turning here from London, will bring fresh instructions in regard to the Afghan boundary question. Concessions are stated to have been made by Russia as well as by England, and, an Igreetnent is expected to be arrived at. 13p1MBAL MONDAY.—lntelligence from a native source states that the Ameer, suspecting the _allegiance of the Jamshedis, near Herat, owing to the visits made to them by a Russian emissary, has imprisoned their Khan, and threatens to execute him unless some of the chiefs of the tribe are brought to Cabul to explain. The Jarnshedis are friendly to the Governor of Penjdeh, and many of their head men have gone to Bala Alingab. The forts defending Herat hays now been repaired, and the crops and adjoining gardens have been cleared. AFFAIRS IN BURMAH.

- RANGOON, SUNDAY.-Mr. CrosthwaAte has arrived at Mandalay, where he will remain for a few weeks before proceeding to Bhatno. During his voyage up the Irra- waddy he found the country between Thayettnyo and Mandalay quiet except the Taundurng,,g,,ee district, which is disturbed. Itamoung, a noted cloccrit leader, who has several times attacked the English troops, surrendered to Brigadier-General Wolseley, who was marching with a force to attack him. After being prisoner for three days, /slgarnoung was allowed to escape, and is at large at the head of his band. The Alaungpra pretender has again assembled a large body of dacoits at Pymalwin. A column has been despatched to attack him. FATHER M‘GLYNN AND THE POPE.

Naw YORK, TOESDAY.—Father Mc.Glynn, speaking at Milwaukee, last night, said he bad heard that he was to be excommunicated, but that would not cause him to alter the course he was pursuing. He still believed him- self to be a good Catholic, and would not admit that the Pope had any right to deprive him of Church fellowship on the sole ground of his holding certain views on politi- cal economy. He had fulfilled his duties as a priest, and he would continue to fulfil his duty according to his conscience as an American citizen and a Catholic.

PESTR, TM:STMT.—lntelligence from Jasz Bereny states that during the drill of some mounted sappers at that place a dynamite cartridge exploded, killing four officers and 16 men on the spot, and injuring 19 others. THEATRE DESTROYED.
MADRID, Tursoar.—The principal theatre at Caceres was destroyqd by fire yesterday. The inmates escaped. DISASTROUS SUBSIDENCES.—TWENTY FAMILIES DROWNED.

BERNE, WEDNESDAY.—The a-nTaTi-canton of Zug, one of the most central and thickly populated of Switzerland, has been tilled with consternation by a series of disastrous sub. aidences which are taking place on Lake Zug. Several newly-constructed Quays at the town of Zug, on the eastern shore of the lake, dissappeared suddenly beneath the water, which is famous for its depth, last night. twenty houses, with the whole of their occupants, principally workpeople, perishing. The subsidences continued through the night until this morning. ELECTION OF A PRINCE FOR BULGARIA.

On Mpnday Dublin Corporation held a meeting, th% /Lord Mayor presiding. As it was understood' that the question of the Mayoralty would be decided at the: meeting, the galleries were filled with spectators, and; crowds were assembled round the doors unable to gain' admittance. The appearance of Mr. Sexton an his sup— . . . . .

porters was the signal for loud and prolonged cheers.. After some preliminary, business had been distaxaed of Mr. Dawson, ex-Lord Mayor, proposed that Mr. Sexton be Lord Mayor for next year. Ile said the question wasp one of national, as well as local, importance. He trusted, that nothing would be done to break the unity an& power of the Irish party. Mr. Winstanley, Mr. Sexton's opponent, next rose, and said he had great pleasure in; seconding Mr. Dawson's resolution, that Mr. Sexton bel, appointed Lord Mayor. (Lond applause.) The resolu- tion was carried.

cotresponuent tuts: iliere Is no truth in the statement which has obtained currency to the effect that the Queen intends giving a silver cradle and six guineas to every child born on her Jubilee day. The rumour has, however, caused much unnecessary trouble, about 400 applications having, it is understood, already been made for the gift. Israel Lipski, 22, walking-stick maker, was charged at the Thames Police Court, on Saturday, with the murder of Mrs. Angels, by pouring acid down her throat. The prisoner looked pale. Ire had no coat on, and was of a dirty appearance. He is slimly built, and looks boyish. The husband of the deceased, and the landlady having given evidence similar to that adduced before the coroner, the prisoner was remanded for a week. THE QUEEN AND A PATIENT SUFFEEER.—Among the poor people who received gifts at Grimsby, last week. on the occasion of the Queen's Jubilee, was a woman named Ann Lowe, who for the last fifty years has been an invalid confined to her bed. The case was brought to the notice of the Queen, who yesterday sent a cheque for £3 for the old lady, "who has spent a Jubilee in patient suffering."

div.head: CURRENT POLITICS.
div.p: CURRENT POLITICS.

Mr. John Morley, M.P., has joined the Free, Land League, and was added on Saturday to the list of vice- presidents. Mr. Edmund Routledge will be the Gls.dstonian Liberal candidate for North Paddington. Mr. Routledge unsuc- cessfully contested North Kensington at the last general election.

It is understood that the Hon. Alan de Tatton Egerton Will succeed Lord Mar..heramorne (Sir J. M‘Garel Hogg) as the representative of the Metropolitan Board of Works in the House of Commons. The Nationalist members intend to raise on the Irish Estimates a debate on the action of Captain Plunkett in superseding the Mayor of Cork, and in refusing to attend the recent meeting of magistrates. .

The Executive Committee of the Brixton Liberal Association have unanimously recommended Mr. James Hill, of the Hawthornes, Clapham-road, and Queen Vic- toria-street, president of the associationj as the 14._,Lal candidate, subject to his acceptance by the Brixton Liberal Four Hunaferat, pith lie meeting at once to be called. Mr. Hill has consented to stand should he be ap- proved of.

It is reported that the Irish National League in America will hold a Convention this year at St. Louis as soon as Possible after the passage of the Coercion Bill. It is said that the leaders of the organisation at Chicago are arranging the matter, and hope to be able to carry the day as they did at the last Convention. In the coming Convention another effort will be made by New Yorkers, in conjunction with anti-administration people all over the country, to defeat the Chicago and Nebraska men, and place their own men at the head of affairs. The Hornsey Liberal and Radical Association, at a numerously attended meeting of its council, has decided to contest the seat vacated by Sir J. M'Garel Hogg, Bart., on his elevation to the peerage, and Mr. Horatio Bottomley (Gladstonian Liberal), of Catherine-street, Strand, and Clapham, has been unanimously selecteciby the Council as the Liberal candidate. The council of the Hornsey Conservative Association have selected Mr. H. C. Stephenß, the well-known ink manufacturer, as the Conservative candidate. In the election of 1885, when the electorate numbered 10,648, Sir James M'Garel Hogg (C) was returned by 4,619 votes, Lord Kensington (I;) receiving 3,299, the Conservative majority, without any question of Unionism then to influence it, thus being 1,320. At the general election in 1886, Sir J. M'Garel liiogg was returned unopposed.

div.head: SPALDING DIVISION ELECTION.-LIBERAL VICTORY.
div.p: SPALDING DIVISION ELECTION.-LIBERAL VICTORY.

The result of the polling in the Spalding Division of Lincolnshire, on Friday, was declared on,Saturday as follows :—Stewart, 5,110; Tryon, 4,363; Liberal majority, 747. Although during the greater part of the day it was thought the poll would be a lighter one than at the pre- vious elections, the result has shown it was heavier bven than in 1885. At the first election for the Spalding division, when the Conservatives won by 78, there were 9,238 votes polled: and at the second, when they won by 288, there were 8,834. On Saturday there were 9473. The greatest excitement prevailed in the Divi- sion, where the result of the election was a complete sur- prise. Mr.' Stewart addressed his supporters, congratu- lating them upon their victory. Mr. Halley Stewart arrived in the lobby of the House of Commons at four o'clock on Monday afternoon, accam- panied by Sir U. Kay-Shuttleworth and Mr. Schnadhorst. Mr. Stewart was warmly greeted by a large concourse of members, among them being Mr. P. Stanhope, Mr. T. B. Potter, Mr. Arnold Morley, Mr. Jacoby, and Mr. Sum- mers. About the same time Mr. Mahony and Mr. J. O'Connor arrived, accompanied by a deputation of the farming electors of the division desirous to see the new member take his seat.

The Tones were most terribly taken aback by the de- claration of the poll at Spalding.. A handsome carriage with four grey horses, and outriders dressed in pink costumes, were imported into Spalding early on Satur- day morning, which, it had been arranged, were to convey Admiral Tryon as M.P. for the Spalding Division through the principal streets of the town in a triumphal procession. Huge placards bad been printed bearing the words, "Farewell Halley, for the third and last time," ready for posting on the hoardings. A number of wreaths of red roses had also been formed, which it was in- tended should be hung across the Market-place. This ostentatious confidence had a depressing effect upon Mr. Halley Stewart's supportersovith the exception of a few, who had observed a decided improvement in the polling at all the stations in the south of the division. Thus Liberals and Tories alike, who assembled in the Market-place to hear the result to the number of about two thousand, were fully prepared to hear Mr. Stewart's third defeat announced. The effect of the announce- ment that the Liberal candidate had obtained 747 majority upon the crowd was extraordinary, and such a scene as was then witnessed has never before been ex- perienced at an .election in Spalding. The pink favours disappearTd rapidly, while the almost frantic cheering of the victorious party was kept up for several minutes without cessation.

MR. BRIGHT ON HOME RULE. Mr. Bright, having had his attention called to an extract recently, published from a speech delivered by him to the Cork Farmers' Club 21 years ago, which said, "If you had a Parliament on College Green, clearly the tenantry of Ireland, with the present feeling in Ireland, would be able to force that Parliament to any measure of justice they desired," writes :—" What I said was true. and I have nothing to retract. The same may be said of Scotland and Wales, and of the great counties of Lancashire and Yorkshire. But it does not follow that it would be wise to establish so many parliaments in order to give special influence to special portions of our population."
