THE Government have suffered another defeat in the House of Commons. The other day it was the leader of the House who went wrong on the question of the Ship Canal Inquiry; this time it is the Honig SECRETARY who has made a mull of it in a matter of public morals. Mr. MATHEWS showed himself purblind and obstinate in refusing an inquiry into what is known as the case of Miss CASS, and as a result of his wrong-headedness the Government were defeated on Tuesday night by a majority of five in a House of over three hundred mem- bers. Briefly stated, the facts of thecase are as follows :—A young milliner named Miss CASS was arrested ingßegent-street by a con- stable on the night of the Jubilee celebration, and was brought next day before Mr. NEW- TON, a stipendiary magistrate, on a charge of soliciting prostitution. Miss CASS emphati- cally denied tne charge, and her employer testifi d to her good character. The case broke down, but in dismissing the young woman the magistrate took upon him- self to say that he believed she was out for an improper purpose, and then he added, "if you are an honest girl, as you say you are, don't walk in Regentistreet at night, for if you do, the next time you are brought here after this caution you will be sent to prison or fined." Assuming the gitl's innocence, and there is every reason to believe her inno- cent, for she had only been in London two months, could anything be m6re infamous than this speech of Mr. NEwrosr ? Instead of protecting her, he heaped insult upon her. And how monstrous to suggest that no young woman has a right to walk ° in Regent-street at nivht, except at .the risk of being ''sent to prison or fined I" The HoAts SECRETARY would not pledge himself to an inquiry, be- cause, as he contended, it involved the question of perjury on the part of the con- stable And what if it did ? Is it not desirable that perjurers should be found out and sent to prison ? or is the gaol only for' respectable young women who venture at night into Regent-street ? me. SMITH, in supporting Mr. MATHEWS, made bad worse by saying it could not be a case of mistake on the part of the constable, and that the proposed inquiry involved more important issues than the character of a young woman. But the House was not disposed to take the official callous view that the character of a policeman is everything, and that of a young woman nothing. The Liberal Unionists, as represented by Mr. CHAMBERLAIN and Mr. CAINE, took the side of Miss CASS, and Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL pretty plainly in- formed the HostE SECRETARY that he had shown himself in this matter pedantic and ' illogical. The House thought so, too, and in the end made a stand in favour of j public morality by putting the Government in a minority. The blow seems to have been a I staggering one; and it was thought, in the ; first instance, that the ROUE SECRETARY would resign. But he has thought better of it. Mr. SMITH came down to the House on Wednesday, and announced that, after what had happened the previous day, the Govern- ment had decided that there should be a full and impartial inquiyy into thewhole facts of the case. The magistrate is to be asked by the LORD CHANCELLOR to make an explana- tion as to his conduct; and if the evidence warrants such a course the policeman will be prosecuted. There is mason now to hope that justice will be done ; for the present House of Commons, had, as it is, better than the present Government.

THE Warrington Library Committee would seem to be determined, so far as they are I concerned, that 'Warrington shall not be favoured with a Free Library. There has been a good deal of fencing with the ques- tion, but they have been met at every point, and, as it is now apparent that the present committee will not move in the matter, it i will be for the ratepayers to determine tbe issue by electing representatives who are willing to carry out their wishes. It is worth remembering that from the first IVr. BEA- -1 MONT, who is the ch iirman and has shown himself the autocrat of the Library Commit- tee, has been opposed to the Principle of making the Lending Library free. With him, lit is not a question of ways and means ; he ' does not believe in the boas of the rate- payers going to the homes of the ratepayers. I He is opposed to the proposed change. and Ihe has all along honestly said so. Other members of the committee profess to be in 'favour of such a Free Library as is possessed 'by every town by which Wank gton is stir- rOunded ; but they are paralt rid in the pre- sence of the chairman. The wttd appears to have been passed round that "nothing can be done so long as Mr. Beamont lives." The

phrase has become stereotyped;and the odd thing is that those who use it do not seem to see how deroaatory it is to the chairman of the Library Committee. He is a stumbling block, it is implied, but he is not to be re- moved, except by death. As to this, however, we shall see. If the people of Warrington are in earnest, as we believe they are, in de- manding that there shall be a remedy for the injustice' un ler which they have so long suf- fered, they will not let the next election pass by without making such a change in the re- presentation as will effect a change in the Library Committee. They must be prepared to say to the committee as Garnhetta said to IVlAcMAttort " Submit or resign." If the committee are incapable of providing a Free Library as is doue in a hundred towns with a penny rate, let them be good enough to retire, and make way for those who can. Hap- pily, the question is one which does not necessarily involve party politics ; every rate- payer, Tory or Radical, is interested in getting his money's worth ; and it is to be foped the inhabitants as a whole will unite in demanding that a resolute effort be made to make . the Library free. , It does not seem to be any use arguing; for the argument has hitherto been all on one side. It has been shown again and again that it is idle to pretend that the dif- ficulty is one of ways and 'means. The Deputation which waited upon the represen- tives of the Library Committee went into details based upon local and general statis- -1 tics to show how the extra cost from making the Library free could be and would be fully met. It was urged as a difficulty that the change should not be of a tentative or tem- porary character; so by way of beating the Committee out of the last ditch, Mr. MONKS wrote the letter, which will be found in another
"TOUCH AND GO."

• Yesterday the preamble of the new Ship Canal Bill was admitted by the house of Lords Committee to be•proved. It is a mat- ter of caurse to say that, after this, there will be no difficulty about getting the bill through the House of Lords.

Prince Henry of Battenberg has been ap- pointed lieutenant colonel in the army ; but from a statement made in the House of Com- mons, on Tuesday, it would seem that " there is no intention of giying him any employment whatever." This puts the case pretty plainly ; Princes in the army are for ornament—:tot for use.

There ha 3 to be another appeal in the Bell- Cox case. Everybody has heard of " the perils which environ the man who meddles with cold iron," but they are as nothing to the perils of law by which the person i sur- rounded who tries to bring a Ritualist par- son to book. Disestablishment would sim- plify the issue very much.
Mr. Goschen professes to be indifferent about the Home Rule victory at Spalding : for what is, as he puts it, an isolated vic- tory in an agricultural district ? " He always
had a coWem- pt for the agricultural labourer, and did his level best to prev,mt him having a vote. And now the labourer is quits ; tie shows his contempt for Mr. Goschen—and all his letters.

As Alderman Pickmere, the Mayor of War- rington. is a Conservative, he has done a graceful thing in appointing Alderman Holmes, who is a Liberal, to be the Deputy- Mayor. It would help to make the municipal machine run smoothly if this practise were generally adopted ; it is so admirably calcu- lated to lessen friction.

The vacant plot of . land in Bridge•street certainly gives Warrington a vacant look. But if there are no buyers the Corporation cannot sell. It takes at least two to make a I bargain. Come, hurry up, you who are thinking of" new and eligible premises," make your offers, down with the dust, and help to 're- duce the rates.

*lt seems that a judge of the County Court has no power to compel the Rev. T. R. Matthews to give a full account of the money he has received and paid in connection with the school at Earlestown. Perhaps he will now furnish the account without prossure. It is usual for people who have a reputation for fair-dealing to give the fullest details as to how they have spentother people's money.

The Runcorn School Board are justiEed in feeling annoyed at the fact that the Board of Guardians have no inquiry officer at work at the present mom-,nt. pending some nego- tiations as to the school fees question. If it be true that certain children of the pooi are unable to attend school, because of a hitch in the arrangement to pay school fees, it is obvious that the Guardians are neglect- ing their duty.

The collector of the Runcorn Board of Guardians likes to have plenty of time to do a thing. It is nearly two years since he was requested to present his books and furnish a statement of accounts. It is not yet done, but the Board have at last awoke to the fact that the collector is treating them with con- tempt. They ought to have made the dis- co Very before, but better late than never. It is bad for thecommunity when,in such cases, ser- vants become masters.

We don't know how many of the County Constabulary have been made ill- by being compelled to wear heavy helmets and heavy coats in the hottest of hot weather ; but we are quite sure that not a few of them have been made miserable. It makes one perspire to look at them. Poor fellows! It is a won- der there is anything left of them, consider- ing that "melting moments" have hal to be endured for hours, and days, and weeks.

John Hogan, cooper, St. Helens, has been getting himself in trouble with the London and North-Western Railway Company. He despatched three and a half tons of staves to Hanley, but made out a consignment which represented the weight as one ton, and paid carriage for one ton only. The Bench ordered him to pay three times the amount of the balance owing to the Railway Com- pany, and mulcted him also in costs. A dealer who does not know the difference be- tween i ton and 3i tons must exoectto suffer fot his ignorance.

Mr. Atherley-Tones, who moved the ad- journment of the debate on Tuesday, and scored such a success in the defeat of the Government in the Cass case, is the son • of the late Mr. Ernest Jones, whose memory Is so dear to Reformers. He represents the North-West Division of Durham, and, like his father, he is a barrister.

The Tory papers are angry with the Go- vernment for the mess they have made of it in the case of Miss Cass. The "Standard" says they have only themselves to thank, for they "clung with obstinacy" to a " radically false position." "The Morning Post" does not hesitate to say that "the result has been a most damaging defeat, which the exercise of a small modicum of common sense and nrdinary judgment would have avoided." For once we agree with the "Morning Post : " the Government are lacking in com- mon tense.

There has been quite an exciting "evic- tion" scene at Widnes. An attempt was made to serve a distress w.drrant for arrears of rent at a house in Alford-street, when the occupant. Isabella Callighan, turned out the bailiff who presented himself, and, bolting the door, assaulted the others with boiling water from the bedroom window. The water finished, she threw the kottie, and inflicted a serious wound on the head of a bailiff. She

It is a matter of course to say th ' Assizes. offer was not accepted; it would have been the same, we believe, if it hao been £5 000 instead of 2500 The question is not one of j the means, but of the will to do the right thing. It is no use beating about the bush; Mr. BEAmorfr blocks the way; and we again ask him to say if we misrepresent him in affirming that he is opposed to the principle of a Free Lending Library. He has a right, of course to his views, however antiquated they may be, but when it comes to a question of imposing his views upon a whole community, the inhabitants, on the other hand, have a right to say that the world has moved in this matter whilst he has stood still, and that they are not content with what was thought good enough when GEORGE the Third was king.

RUNCORN AND THE LIVERPOOL WATERWORKS RILL.— The Liverpool Waterworks and Improvement Bill on Thursday passed the House of Lords Committee. The Run- corn Boatel ot Commissioners a few yeers ago obtained the insertion of a clause giving them the right to draw water front the mains of the Vyrawy scheme, and the Runcorn, Weston, and Halton Waterworke sought to have this set aside. The law clerk (Mr. W. H. Linaker) was therefore I instructed to brief counsel, and with Mr. Speakman he was I appointed to represent the Commissioners in London during the progress of the Bill. Mr. Speakmen and Mr. Linaker were empowered to take such steps as they considered ad- visable to protect the interests of the town. The services of Mr. Pope, Q.C., were secured on behalf of the Board, and he made a speech before the Lords Committee yester- day. We are glad to say the clause was retained. FATALL ACCIDENT 'AT DUTTON Woantronsts —tan Tues- day, at Dutton Workhouse, an inquest was held by Mr. R. White, deputy-coroner, relative to the death of Thomas Jpfliries, a painter, who met with a fatal accident on Monday while following his occupation at the Workhouse premises. Mr. John Garrett was present to watch the case for Messrs. Kirkham, painters. Runcorn, by whom deceased was eill- ployed.—Mxry Jeffries, wife of deceased, said that he hue. band was 49 years of age and lived at Acton Bridge.—Jane r Millingtonon inmate of the Workhouse, said that while ehe Was sitting on the steps of the dieing hall deceased was on a long ladder painting a building onposite. She heard him shout "Ob. dear," and then he fell to the ground. He was picked up and taken to-the hospital. The ladder did not fall.—Thomas Fletcher, of Briscoe.street, Runcorn, said he wee foreman of the uainters engard at the Work- house. The ladder was a new one and deceased • fixed it himself.—Margaret Ann Rodgers, nurse at the Workhouse hospital, geld that deceased was brought to the hospital shout twenty minutes to elevrn., He was quite unconscious when brought in and the usual remedies were applied. tie died about bait AR hour afterwards. The injuries appeared to be about the spine and the ribs.—A verdict of " Acciden- tal death" was' returned. RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUrHORITY —The fort- nighty meeting of this Authority was held at Dutton Work- house on Tuesday afternoon: ' There were present Messes I MRra(presiding), Aaron, Knowles, Stokes, Lewis, Strait'', ac and Rev. J. Lockwood ; Mr. H. L naker (cle-k), teyldr, e Or. Adams (medical officer) —sledical Officer's Report : The Medical Officer's report was relit It contained nothing of importaoce with the exception that there had been a else I of scarlet fever at Kekewick.—Dr. Adams said the \case was convalescent when reported to him, and it had been a very ; mild one.—Compliments to the Local Government Board: The Clerk stid that the committee appointed to consider I the letter from the Local Government Board, read at the ' last meeting, with reference to milkshops and dairies had met that dav, and he read' the notes of a reply that had been decided upon by the committee. The committee took exception to the requirement of the Local Government Board that 800 cubic feet space should be provided in a Allmon for each cow.—The Chairman said he thought this a ridiculous provision.—Mr. Aaron said the cows would be starved in winter if the obit:mons were made so lerge.—The Clerk said he did not think the man who wrote the letter of the Local Government Board knew what a shippon was.— Mr. Aaron :1 don't think he knows the difference between a cow and a horse.—Mr. Hadfield. said the: independent of the stnpidity.of the Local Government Bo rd's letter' he thought it was a very improper thing that they should have been so many months as thy had been In answering the commanications of the Rural Sanitary Authority —Oa the motion of Mr. Knowles it was agreed that the reply sag. gelded by the committee shodld be sent to the Local Gov- erment Board.—This was all the business of pnblic in- terest.

_ ROYAL LIVER FRIENDLY SOCIETY, WIDNES DISTRICT. —On Wednesday evening, at Malin' Temperance Hall, Widnes, the first meeting of the members of the Royal I Liver Friendly Society, reaident in Widnes district, was heM for the purpose nf selecting a delegate to attend the general meeting in Liverpool at the end of the present month. The eociety has juet passed through a stormV period of its existence, with the result that its affaire have been placed under the control af anew and popular man• &gement. Under this new management the total weekly collections have increaeed nearly £BOOO. The statement of accounts ahews that during the page year the income was no less than £402718, while £204,425 was paid in claims and grants. The benefit funds have inereneed by £31,011, and now stand at' the large total of £887,795. Compared with 1885 there has been a saving in the working ex- penses of the society of no less than £11,248, •a fact that reflects great credit upon the new management. Mr. Kilroy.l the Widnes agent, having read a letter to the members, it was reselved on the motion of Dr. McCembridge, seconded by Mr. Rowe, that Mr. J. W. Davies take the chair.—The Chairman remarked that it augured well for the future of the society that the members wete now given more fully the power of conducting its affairs, and be trusted that they had seen the end of the grave scandals that had agitated the members in past years.—Mr. Rowe Proposed, and Mr. A. G. Davies seconded a motion that De. McCambrid,e3 should be appointed the delegate of the Widnes district, and it was carried unanimously.—Dr. McCambridge thanked them far the honour they had conferred upon him. He had been a membar of the society for seen years and had taken groat interest in its affairs. The work of reform completed a year ago, he did all its his power to aid, aeri to see that the money of the society was properly spent. (Applause.)—The I proceedings then concluded.

The defendant only touched 'him ' 1 with the whip as a warning.—The Bench considered the case proved, arid Imposed a tine of ss, and costs 16' 6d, A DISORDERLY HOUSE AT RUNCORN : A BRUTAL Fat- Low.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, 3 homes Jannion. a rough-looking fellow, was charged with assisting in the msnagernent of a house of ill fame in ()flows-street, on the 25th June, at:dottier days —Superintendent Honing- worth paid the doff ndant was not the occupier of the house, but his sister, Fanny Jannion. She was a wall-known char- actsr, and a witness who had been sumnionrd had been obliged to leave the neighbourhood through the defendant's illusage. If the magistrates were satisfied that tire d-fend- ant had been assisting in the management of the house, he asked them to give such punishment as would tend to attnip . out the disirderly housm in the town. Evidence wee given by Insprctor Millington, P.C.s Miltitigtun and Dutton, and Mrs Esatua.Jones, showing the character of the house, and the .lefendant'a connection with it.—The Bench. sentenced the defendant to three months' hard labour.-.-Tbe defenat- ant was then charged with assaulting an old woman named Emma Jones, who lives in King-street, and he pleaded guilty. It appeared that at live o'clock on the morning of the 30th ult, the defendant was beating the woman with whom ha cohabited in a most savage manner. and Mrs. Jones remonstrated with him. The defendant threatened "to do the same for her," rind she ran into the house and Inked the door. The defendant, however, burst it op-n and assaulted her in a most brutal fashion by striking her on the head and body with his fist. She had to be treated by Dr. McDougall.—Superintendent Itillinzworth said•ha did not wish to press the case nodally, bat be must state that the defendant was known all over the county as a most violent character, and he bad been cmvicted at Crewe and Chester for assaults at various times.. He was a most brutal and cowardly fellow.—The magistrates sentenced the defendant to a month's hard Itt.ottr. SIR WILLIAM CUNLIFFE. BROORS.—Sir William Cunliffe Brooks, M.P., is progressing most favour- ably under the results of his late accident. For- tunately the honourable baronet was in excellent health. :No. inflammation supervened, and there re- mains only the temporary inconvenience of a disa- bled left arm. BAZAAR AT KINGSLEY.—We would again remind our readers that a bazaar in aid of the endowment of the Church of St. John the Evangelist, will be i held at Belle Mont, Overton Hills, on Thursday,Fri- day, and Saturday next. I Besides a variety of other attractions, on the evenings of Friday and Satur- day "Old English sports" will be held. JUBILEE RELICS AT CADISHEAD.—On the 28th day of June 1837, a party met to celebrate the ac- cession of ale Queen at Rose Bank House, Cadis- head, then occupied by Ur. Henry Hardy. A flag was displayed with a crown upon it, and there are some living who took part in the rejoicings. Miss Alice Hardy was one of the party. She is still liv- ing at the same house, but she is now Mrs Shaw,and on Tuesday, the 22nd June, she had the same flag displayed. She wore, too, the bonnet she had on on -June 28th, 1837. Both have been preserved with grealeare as interesting relics. " AND SIR GILBERT GREENALL.—The member for Warrington has become famous; he is again mentioned by "Punch," but whether it on be called an "honourable mention" we leave our readers to judge. The reference to Sir Gilbert is at the tail end of the following hupourous comment on the new mode of taking a diAsion, and is from Toby's Essence of Parliament:—" Ritchie has in- vented new way of taking Division. Members as anxious to try it as nursery of children to handle new toy. At first some little difficultY in under- standing it. Members crowded round Ritchie and asked how it was done. 'Nothing easier or clearer,' he said. 'Therb are six doors, whicti We will call A. B, C, D, E, and F. As soon as division bell rings Fis closed. B is' left half open. Members voting Aye' pass through the A door and meet the Noes' coming through D. A and C are then dimultane- ously shut. If B is open, the Ayes' and the Noes, having seen E closed, form in one stream, pass through, and there you are. Don't you see?' Everybody saw quite clearly. Quite .13, pleasure to see Isaac Holden (etat. eighty, but full of youthful vigour) starting off to try the new experiment. Got through all right. But,, half an hour later, Gilbert Greenall found in . recesses of venti- lating cellars, where, he said, he was 'looking for door E."

Whence comes this epidemic of suicides? Receredie- cuasions have named several causes. One,writer charges it to' infidel teachings, holding that hopelessness of a future state 'cripples fortitude for bearing life's ills; another de- clares suffering from the universal business depression, the cause; a third ttributes it to increasing insanity; phy- itician thinks much cf Liao tendency is inherited; while tem- perance advocates lay the responsibility epos strong drink. • Freethinkers have committed suicide, and so have ortho- dox Churchmen; financial straits have beset many, but the wealthy have also taken their life; insanity and dissipation .have preceded saicides and murders. One feature common to almost every such crime chal- lenges attention. Well-nigh every report of suicide and family murder mentions the perpetrator as haying for some time been subject to melancholy. Whences comes this? All recognised medical authorities tell es that the fire which consumes the brain is always kindled by derangements of iodigestion; that good digestion is impossible withou". pure blood, and pure blood is nover known whgn the liver and kidneys are out of order. The property had already been twice offered for sale by auction, and once the Town Clerk had been in negotia- tion. They were always open to an offer, which they would take, if a reasonable one. Last time the property was offered for sale by auction they bad no reason- able bid for any portion of it. He thought the Council must seeifor itself that the state of things was not such as they could wish it to be, owing to the state of trade in the country. The state of trade in the country did not war- rant any shopkeeper to build or anybody to build for shop- keepers. As he had said, however, they were always open to an offer, but they might possibly get a more reasonable price in a few years. A Moment: When the Ship Canal comes. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) Councillor PLAIT: Yes, when the Ship Canal comes. He did not agree with Alderman Harrison that they should sell the property at some price or ether. The committee would do the best they couid fir the ratepayers, and if they thought they could get a better price next year, than by throwing it on the market now they would, keep it till next year. As far as the cost of the property went, 'it had, broadly speaking, cost about the figures they gave to the Council at first—at any rate they did not exceed their esti- mates. They estimated the gross cost would be £3l 000, and it appeared that they had expended £30,941 9s 61. (Laugh- ter.) That was extremely near, but they would see that the committee had not exceeded their estimate. The com- mittee did riot think the present time was favourable for the selling of the property, and, in fact, they did not seem to have any market for it at all. The DEPUTY-MAYOR cud his own impression was that if the Ship Canal came off, the property would go up in value. (Hear, hear.) The minutes of the committee were then confirmed. The minutes of the Sanitary Committee contained the following items :—That the tender of Mrs Charlotte Lunt, for the ensuing three months, for carting ashes. chc., at 63 Pd per day, be accepted. That Mr. Councillor Francomb be appointed a memoer of the Longford ab-Committee. Councillor FRANCOII3 moved, and Councillor GREENING seconded, the adoption of these minutes. Councillor PLATT said he was sorry the chairman of the committee (Alderman Burgess) was not present. Ile had mentioned before the nuisances arising from the intercept- ing depot, and he had complained to the committee in one or two letters. To those letters he had not had an answer from the committee. He had now to complain that the nuisance was getting worse than ever it had been ; it was making people ill in the neighbournood. Unless prompt steps were taken by the Sanitary Committee to amend the etate of matters—if it could be amended—some serious notice would have to be taken of it by the property-owners of the locality. It was becoming a very serious matter. He had kept quiet as long as possible. but he could keep quiet no longer. He seriously warned the Sanitary Committee that they would get into very serious difficulties unless the matter was remedied without delay. Councillor BARKER askekl to what depot Councillor Platt referred. Councillor PLXTT said he referred to Lythgee's-lane depot. He was only speaking of the one though he had no doubt the other was in pretty much the same condition. Councillor GIIEENALL asked If it was true that there had be-n a breakbown at Longford depot ; why Councillor Francomb had b,en appointed a member of the Longford SnhecOmmittse ; if ark employe had been discharged from Longford; and also what the amount of damage to the machinery was. Councillor FRANCOMR, in replying, said that the (km. mitten were most anxious to stop any nuisance lat,ing com- mitted in the neighbourhood of Lyttigoesdane. A fortnight ago they certaiulv had a little breakdown at Longford which certainly upeet their arrangements at the interceping depots and they thought that when that was put right there would be no more cause for complaint. Had the chair- man been present he would have been very much upset on hearing that even now the thing was not cured. As far as Longford deporwas concerned they certainly had 'hal a breakdown. Councillor Greenall asked why he (Councillor Francomb) was put on as a member of the sub-committee and to that he could only say that it was at the suggestion of SOM3 members of the Committee, but if the Council would relieve hint he would be much obliged to them. (Laughter). The minutes were then confirmed.

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 9. 1887.
PAVING AND SEWERAOR CONHITTER.--Y/TH WILDERSPOOL AND LA TCHFORD ROADWAYS. _

The Paving o and Sewerage Committee recommended,l that sevrers be laid in Thelwall-lane and Forster-street in Accordance with requests contai.ed in applications from F. Rouen and Robert Curran. That the Corporation enter into a contract with the local authority of the county of Chester for the repair and maintenance by the Corporation of Wilderspool and Latchford roadways for the further period of seven years, at £340 per annum. That the tender of Mr. William Williams for taking op and relaying sewers in Dial and Whittle-streets, at £44 4e 11d, Las accepted. , That the tender of Mr. Thomas Pilkington for netting ac- cording to schedule of distances, and his alternative offer to supply horses and drivers at 6s 84 per day, be accepted, the Corporation to have the option of relinquishing either of such offers. _ . .

Alderman DAWES, in movit.g the confirmation of the , minutes, said that seven years ago they entered into a con- tract with the county authorities for the repair and main- tenance of the roads named in the minnies. It had turned out that they had spent quite as much money on the main- tenance of the roads as tnev bad been paid, but they had a double advantage in keeping the contract. because the pri- mary question for them to consider was haviug good ro ids in that part of the town. Since the reign of shout Henry VII the county authorities bad been liable for the repair of the roads, and that had been the good luck of the town, be- cause the greater part of the roads were within the borough and the responsibility, therefore, attached to the county authorities. The county authorities would be sure to look upon the roads as county roads, whereas the Corporation knew they were purely town roads, and if they could g.t acorn of money equivalent to maintain them as town roads he considered they were doing a good thing to the town in getting the contract renewed. The increase traffic neer the two roads during the last seven years had been in- creased 25 per cent, arid that was a most startling fact. Councillor ILSIITOA seconded the confiratatitm of the minutes.

Councillor PLATT was glad the Corporation had again taken over the repair of the roads, because it would be misfortune to the inhabitants of Warrington if the roads were treated as purely county roads. He could triite us- derstand that the Committed had allowed the condition of the roads to go down whilst the bargain was in contempla- tion, as as a matter of business he supposed. (Laughter.) Alderman Deviss.—Tt is quite true. Councillor Purr —I am very glad yen have concluded the bargain, because I have no doubt we shall get them put into a proper state of repair without delay. Councillor H. ROBERTS said he felt gratified to see the resolution with reference to tee tender for carting, because he thought it was the result of a resolution adopted by the Council a short time ago of potting everything up to con- tract that could be pot tip. When they remembered that the Corporation paid 83 a day previously for every horse and ma 2 they employed, and now is 4d a day less,, they would neethere was a very c -nsidcreble item of saving. . .
- ----- Councillor BROWN obaerved that the 8a a-day included - • - -

something beyond a man and horse. It included the cart, the wear and tear of which was a consideration. The com- mittee had had this subject before them for several irootbs past, and it was not owing to any outside influence that the committee bad entered into the present arrangement.
The minutes were agreed to. THE FREE LENDING LIBRARY QUESTION.
The mi-nn—tee-O-f--a meeting of this committee stated that

the following letter was re-ad :—"Brooklande, Warrington. 12th May, 1887. Mr, Alderman Webster, Mr. R. Davies, and Mr. W. Owen. Gentlemen,—ln your report to the Muissom Committee re Free Lending Library, and which has been accepted by them and the Town Council as repre- senting all that can be said against the scheme, it narrows the subject to a mere question of finance. We submitted certain figures which you distrust, but ye have sufficient faith to believe that if fairly tried they will work out sub- stantially correct. With a view to removing this doubt, I am authorised to say that a gentleman, on behalf of the deputation from the Jubilee Committee, is prepared to guarantee the amount as set forth by us for the next five years. If necessary ha is prepared to deposit Ccrootation Bonds to any extent you may decide up to 5.500, which will be ample to cover our figures if they should fail alto- gether. You are authorised to make this proposition to the Museum Committee at their meeting on Friday, and we hope it will be the means of settling this question to the satisfaction of all. We think it would only be reasonable that we should suggest one or two names to be on the committee- so long as the guarantee is' required. Signed on behalf of the deputation of the Jubi- lee Committee, yours truly, F. Motrirs." The following report was presented by the Sub-Committee ap- pointed at the last meeting :—ree Sub-Committee having carefully considered Mr. Monks' letter appended hereto are of opinion :-1. That a free lending library would augment the expenditure to an extent which it is difficult to estim- ate. 2. That they c inner recommend the proposed change upon any personal guarantee; and, that the change, when. ever effected, must not be of a temporary or tentative char- acter. 3. That unless the amount of rate can be lecreased, or other permanent provisions made for the additional ex- penditure, they, as business men, regret that they do not see their way to report in favour of the views of the ,depu- tation. The Sub Committee wish to add, with reference to

the opening passage of Mr. Monks' letter, to the effect that I their report bad been accepted by the Committee and the Town Council " s representing all that could be , said against tt e scheme." that this WAS not their view, inasmuch as they did not consider it within their powers to enter upon the general quastion, or to do more than report upon the statement laid before them by the deputation. Signed. S. M. WEBSTER, ROBERT DAVIES. WILLIAM OWEN.' —The Committee resolved that the above report be adopted and entered on the minutes, that the best thanks of this Com- mittee be given to Mr. William Barlow and Mr. Chyles Chorley for loans of works of art which have now been re- turned, and that the tender of Mr. Mounfield for a store cabinet be accepted. Twenty books were ordered to be purchased. The following return for May was presented : Visitors to the museum, 3,419. increase 53 per cent; hooks Issued in reading r-om, 1,271. increase 2 per cent; bsoks betted in lending depertment, 1,714, increase 4 per cent, compared with May, 1886. The minutes were confirmed, without discussion, on the motion of Alderman WEBSTER. seconded by Councillor GREENALL.

div.head: ECHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE.
div.p: ECHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE.

This committee reported that 33 cases had been inquired into by the Beard of Guardians, and school fees allowed in 32 cases for 69 children. Nine cases had been taken before the magistrates, when fines were inflicted in eight cases and one sent to the ship "Clio." 17 cases were brought before the committee and dealt AO. Alderman WEBSTER proposed, and Councillor Frardirru seconded the adoption of the report. Councillor PLATT said that at the 'last meeting it was promised on behalf of the committee that some steps should be taken to remedy the grievance about half-timers at school; he asked had that been done, or was it in the power of the committee to remedy it? Councillor Joralcr said that as it was now the school holidays it had been found to be impossible at present to move in the matter. Councillor Dnrow did not think that the committee had got all the power they should have; this was a question that they had been dealing with for five years. Alderman WEBSTER remarked that the subject of the charges that had been made for half-timers had been over and over again before the committee. Parents complained that their children, when they became half-timers, were at one school told that the fee would be dounle what it was under ordinary circumstances. This was, he mentioned, confined to one school. The practise had been discon- tinued for some time. There could be no doubt that if the cause of complaint was continued by any school, a School Board would be insisted upon in the borough, which was a serious matter to consider. He thought, however, that for the present at any rate the matter was at an end ; he hoped it would continue so.
The minutes were then approved. CEMETERY COMMITTEE.

The minutes of this committee were confirmed on the motion of Alderman HARRISON, seconded by Councillor Bitowtr. In the report it was stated that the interments for the past six weeks were :—Adults, 47; minors, 66; stillborn and premature, 18; and for the corresponding period last year, adults, 52 ; minors, 50; stillborn and premature, 18. The receipts for the past leer weeks were £93 12a 53, and for the corresponding wrind last year, £9O 17s.

OAS COMMITTEE.-PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND INTEREST.

At a meeting held on the 10th June, the Borough Trea- surer submitted the following statement of the amount required for the payment of annuities and interest, which were ordered to be paid. Half-year's annuity on 1,435 old shares, £1,435: htlf-year's annuity on 2,839 new shares, £993 133; half-year's interest on -£15,500 (600 at £4 per cent., and £14,900 at £3 103 per cent.), £272 15s; half- year's interest on £41,400 (17 500 at 4 per cent., and £23,900 at 31- per cent.) £765 53; a year's instalment for the redemption of annuities, £2040; total, £5,509 131.—1 t was resolved that the pre of gas used for illuminating pur- poses on the nights of the 20t'a and 213 t June be reduced to one-half; that the tender of Mr. William Williams for ex- cavating pipe trenches, according to schedule of sizes and specific stion, and his tender for plying at 3!2-cl per square yard, be accepted, acd that the tender of Mr. R. A. Naylor for oak cut to Biz-, at 3s per cubic foot, be accepted. The average illuminating power of the gas for the past four weeks was repotted to be equal to 18 candles at both works.

Alderman HOLMES, in proposing the confirmation of the mieutes, referred to the payments of the annuities and in- terest, and slid that last year the cost was £5,670. and this year it was £5,509, being a reduction of about £l6O. They would ss by that that the dr ht was being extinguished, and that the amount of interest they had to pay was being an- nually decreased. The CLERK read a letter from the Local Government Board containing an extract from the report of their in- spector, Mr. Steve:-e, with regard to an inspection of the Workhouse. The extract was as follows :—" The Porter also has a daughter here." He (the clerk) did not know what that meant. The Guardians did net provide any pro- visions for the porter's daughter.—Mr. BLACICHURST said if she did not cost the Board anything he did not see why they should isterfere.-,-It was agreed that the Clerk should reply that the Porter was • a widower and although his children lived with him they were not provided with any provisions at the cost of the Board.

ACKNOWLEDGMENTS.

The Matron of the Workhouse (Mrs. Ward) or behalf of the sick inmates acknowledged with thanks the gift of a quantity of fhwers brought b-r the ladies from the Wesley- an Chapel, Moore. The Workhouse Master also reported that a.number ef the inmates had requested him to express their gratitude to the Board of Guardians for the great treat they enjoyed on jubilee day.

div.head: OBJECTION TO THE UNIFORM.
div.p: OBJECTION TO THE UNIFORM.

Mr. Hattneson eaid be had a matter to submit to the Board, ft was this; supposing an inmate of the Work- house wanted to go out for a day would he be permitted to go in his private clothes. Ife had jest been speaking to the Master on the subject, and he said he did not feel justi- fied in letting an inmate go out in his private clothes with- out the sanction of the Board. His inquiry was based up- on a case that occurred on jubilee day. An old man in the house—i person of exceedingly respectab'e connections— wanted to go out on jubilee day, and he applied to the Mas- ter for permission to go out in his own private clothe', which in his (Mr. Harrison's) opinion was a very natural request, bat the Master replied that he bad no power to al- low an inmate to go out in his private clothes. The man did not complain about the Master, but ,he thought it was bard that be should be compeiled to go dot with the stigma of pauperism on his back. The Consolidated Orders did not mentioned the subject except that they said when an in- mate went before the ,juetices to give evidence he could go I in his private clothes if he wished. He (Mr. Harrison) would ask the Board if they would be disposed to give the master discretionary power to allow a well-behaved, respec• table inmate te so out in his private clothes.—Mr. BLACK. HURST quite agreed with Mr. Harrison's suggestion; its thought they might safely allow he master discretionary power.—Mr. GREENING said that before Mr. Ward came to the Workhouse inmates used to go out in their own clothes; he had seen paupers Out of the Workhouse re- peatedly in their own clothes. He also supported the dllg- gesti.n that the master have discretionary power.—The WORKHOUSE Manna, having been called into the rdom, said that he had followed his previous practice in declining to allow an inmate to go out in his private clothes. Daring ' his 14 years' experience he had never allowed a man to go out of the Workhouse except in his pauper clothes.—Mr. DARBYSEIRE opposed the proposal to give the mester die- cretionary power. He thought it was better that the in- mates should go out in their uniform, and he did not see why they should feel it any stigma upon them to wear clothes provided for them by the ratepayers.—Mr. Jorzeter suppor- ted the suggeitien of Mr. Harrison. He did not see any reason why a man should be forced to parade his regimen- tals before his friends, and particularly, as in the case men- tioned, when the. man had Been better days.—Mr. STRANGE asked if the proposal did not apply to females.—Mr. JOLLEY: Both male and female.—Mr. Gensox asked if there had not been a resolution passed that paupers should go out only in their Workhouse clothes. There bad been a case in which a woman had been let oat in her own clothes and she had disappeared, leaving her children behind. Several men had also gone in that way.—The CLERK said that when persons went out in their own clothes and did not return they could not be prosecuted—Mr. Hemasote thought if they gave the master discretionary power be would not let anyone go out who was likely to run away.— The Cetaeumeer suggested that it should be the rule ot the Workhouse that inmates go out in the uniform of the UOIOE, but that the wager be allowed a diecretionary power to relax tl-e rule where he thought it could be safely made. He would make a proposition to that effect.—Mr. GREEN- ING seconded the proposal.—Mr. RATCLIFFE asked where they would draw the line ; if they let one inmate out and not another there would be a great deal of jealousy. It would open the door to a very injurious system, and he objected to the master being given an arbitrary power of the kind the:: proposed.—Mr. DAREYSHIRE Proposed as an amendment that no alteration be made in the system of not allowing any inmate to go out except in his workhouse clothes.— Mr. RATCLIFFE seconded the amendment.—On the amend-
meat being put to the vote ten voted in its favour, and as there were only five for the original resolution, the amend- ment was carried. RELIEF TO MF.I\IRERS OF FRIENDLY SOCIETIES.

Mr. ISHERWOOD asked if a pauper inmate of the work- house was receiving relief from a friendly society could the Guardians insist upon payment. —The CLERK said it de- pended very much upon the rules of the society. They would find that many friendly societies had provided a rule that in case any person belonging to the seciety should be granted relief from the poor rate the friendly society should not be forced to pay. if those rules were confirmed by the officer in London appointed for the purpose, he was afraid the friendly society had an answer for them In court. They might take it as a rule that the matter depended on the rules of the friendly society. If there was no such rule then they could recover from the friendly society.— Mr. IsmEnwoon said he was not prepared to give a full ex- planation, but they had hod a man in the workhouse who had been drawing a certain sum and giving it to a relative. —The CLERK said that if Mr. Isherwood would give them norticutars of a case of that kind he would write to the frbmdly society about it —The matter then dropped. There was no otha business of public interest.

ACCIDENT ON AN IRISFIRAILIVAY.-oWing, it is stated, to some failure in the brake action the mail train from Cork to Bantry, due at the latter station at six a.m., met with a serious accident on Thursday morning when running into Bantry. The engine left the rails, and the driver and fireman were thrown r)ff, a guard and one passenger being also injured. Ihe first-named three, who were the most seriously hurt, were taken to the hospital. The driver and fireman's state is precarious. Ts BOLTON bTRIKE.—The seventeen imported men at the Soho Iron Works, Belton, had a smoking concert pro- vided for them on Wednesday night, and the pleasant change was much appreciated. The men state when en- gaged they were fully aware of the strike, and are at perfect liberty to go out of the works, but prefer to remain inside at present. There are fifty policemen inside the works to guard them when sleeping, and the cooking'arrangeneents are most elaborate. More importations are expected. All the outer walls of the works are barricaded, the place being as in a siege. Replying to Mr. W. Hargroaves. Mr. Hough, chairman of the Men's Committee, points out that Mr. Har- greaves had admitted that there was more work, but it had been taken at a low price, which was unjust to ;he men. who were now getting less wages than in 1851. They will accept Mr. Hargreaves's challenge about wages in Manches- ter if he will confine the radius to three miles cf the Town Hall.
NOTES BY THE WAY.

At Brighton, on Saturday, after a well-contested game, Sussex beat Kent, thtee-quarters of an hour before time, with'seven wickets to spare. The remarkable stand made by Mr A. J. Thornton and Frank fleanae on Friday after- noon gave Kent a fair chance, but the visitors' remaining seven wickets fell on Saturday for 108 more rune, and the 131 runs necessary to win were scored by Sussex on a hard but somewhat worn wicket,for the loss of three of their bats- men. Mr Thornton was batting nearly five hours and a quarter. The only other innings worth mentioning was the Kent captain's useful 35..

In the match bet went Gloucestershire and Yorkshire on Sat- urday, Mr. W. G. Grace fairly eclipsed the somewhat bril- liant batting performances of the earlier stages of the game. Going first wicket down at four, Mr. Grace carried his bat -through the rest of the inning-, and was ultimately not out for a superb schre of HI As far as could be seen, the display was a faultless one; indeed he hardly made a bad stroke, though one hit fell just short of mid-off after he had scored his hundred. In all he was batting just under five hours and a half. His innings was made up of twenty-one 4's, four 3'e, nineteen 2's and forty-nine singles. He was much cheered at the close. Apart from Mr. Grace's re- markable achievement, perhaps the meet noteworthy per- formance was that of Hunter, the Yorkshire wicket-keeper, who made six catches on Saturday. In the two Innings he got rid of nine batsmen. The match, which had lasted nearly three full days, ended in a draw in favour of the home side. In the three complete innings no fewer than 1,007 runs were scored. Notts gained a well earned victory over Lancashire at Nottingham on Saturday. Such a result was only to be expected, as at the 'dose of Friday night's cricket, Lan- cashire, with three good wickets down, wanted 199 runs to save being beaten in a-single innings. Briggs and Robin- son added 70 runs during their partnership, but the others could not offer much resistance to the bowling of the Notts men, and the innings was all over by a quarter to two for

. .=, . 136. Drips, in his dashing 50, hit six 4's, five 3's, and two 2's. Mr. Dixon did a remarkable piece of ,bowling, dis- missing Robinson, Briggs, and Yates with three successive balls, thus accomplishing the hat trick.

- Staffordshire narrowlyr, escaped tone innings defeat at the hands of Cheshire on Saturday. Overnight they were left with 109 runs for seven wickets, against Cheshira 259. The three remaining wickets were disposed of in ten minutes on Saturday for 9 runs, leaving .141 to be got to avert a vie- story for Cheshire by an innings. By hard work they pared the fatal point by 12 runs. This is the first match won by Cheshire thirseason.

The match for the benefit of Harry Butler, the pro, of the St. Helens club,was largely attended on Saturday afternoon. The visitors were Preston. who gave the Sr. Helens men a decisive thrashing in the first match between the two teams at Preston a few weeks ago. The home team hoped to turn the tables on their opponents, but, owing principally to bad fielding, they failed to do this. In a first appearance at the wickets the St. Helens men were out for the poor total of 54 runs," Harry" being the top scorer, with 13 to his credit. The Prestonians started badly, and three of the best bats were dismissed for about ten runs, but the patient and steady batting of Addie and others, the result was soon put beyond doubt, and St. Helens were defeated by 121 runs to 54. A remarkable feature of the play was that the last wicket of the Preston innings realised 41 runs. To play out time St. Helens again went to the wickets and scored 50 runs for the loos of four wickets. The Plateworks team met Liverpool Press on the ground of the first-named, and a capital match was the result. The visitors notched 108 runs, while the glass makers scored 85 for two wickets, C Ripley and P rye be- be' not out with respective scores of 40 and 19. ' The St. Helens Recs. met the Plateworke second team, and on going first to the wickets the "Recs." kept the wickets all day, sc-ring a total of 190 runs, in which .I)bn Wilson figured well with 59 runs to his credit.

THE LADY DOUGLAS TRAGEDY.—In reference to the four men sentenced to death at the Old Bailey last week for the murder of a Malay on board theeship Lady Douglas, the Horne Secretary has advised the Queen to respite the death sentence, and commute it to five years' penal servitude in the case of Captain Cocks, eighteen months in the case of Evans and Gleres, an twelve months in Webstees case. Tens TITHE Wart.—At Rethin, on Wednesday, 31 per- sons were charged with being concerned in the riots at Liangwni on May 27, when the auctioneer and his assist- ants, who had arrived there to carry out sales of cattle seized for tithe; were set upon and severely beaten. "Ap Alwrog," the auctioneer, deposed that he was pelted with eggs and stones, and threatened with death unless he took an oath that he would never again have anything to do with tithe distraints in that district. Other witnesses were ex- amined, and deposed to receiving much injury at the hands of the mob. The ease was adjourned.

Vasbead off ce.Bewsev-street. Warringteo. not later than ten Sir —ln Golborne the removal of night soil has long been oselovic on IMI ednesdav morning, clone voluntarily. Recently the Parochial Committee ten- tiered its removal compulsory, and in dping so have effected a wise and mach-needed reform. The local authority ap- pears, however, to have overlooked a most important part of the arrangement—the time of its removal. To have one's back premises blockaded during the whole day, and a tropi- cal sun filling the air with noxious odours, is not one of the most delightful experiences. and yet this is how matters stand at present. The comfort ci the public Is held amenable to the eoprice or convenience of the persons removing the night soil, and it is quite time the matter was placed upon a more satisfactory basis. Property owners in the town have been compelled to spend money in the removal of troisances much less harmful than those ac- cruing from the present method of removing night soil. Further, any person collecting night soil shonld be com- pelled to use a disinfectant after its removal and to see that all noxious matter is carefully removed. I have found a pestiferous stench arising from spots where night soil has been deposited many days after its removal, and a currory glance has shown that no elort has been made to thorough' 'clean the ground. I feel sure the Parochial Committee will see that the evil is remedied, and so earn the gratitude of many sufferers.—Youre, otze. A RATEPAYER.

TUNNEL MYSTERIES. Sir,—As thelollowing incident is, I think, of interest and importance not only to those who travel over the ?Quechee- ter South Junction and A,ltrincham Ene, but also to all who travel on any system of rail, I trust you will allow me to relate it in the columns of your widely read and influen- tial journal :—One day when. going 'to Manchester by the 12-30 p.m. train from Altrincham, into which I got at Sale, when passing through Old 'Trafford Tunnel I heard an un- usual sound, and on emerging from it, discovered the door on the down line side wideepen, and the compartment full of smoke and steam. Of course I closed it ot once; but what would have been the consequence if a child had been the occupant, and that little one had been leaning against the door? The inevitable result would have been that it would have fallen out, and in all probability killed by the train. passing over it that passed on the down line immediately after I got the door fastened; or it might even have oc- curred to an adult, who, in the sot of closing the window to keep out the steam and fool air, by the impetus of the door swinging open, might have been hurled out on the rails, to be picired up later on and classified as "another tunnel mystery." Evidently the door had not been properly closed at Altrinchatn before the train started, and my ob- ject in troubling you with this is to point out the necessity of each one seeing for himself, that the doors Are securely fastened, more esPocially during the period of the Man- chester, Liverpool, and Saltaira Royal Jubilee Exhibitions, when the trains on the lines round about Warrington, Man- chester, Liverpool, Bradford, and neighbourhood& are like. lv to be overcrowded; and occurrences like the foregoing more or less likely to happen.:-..Y0ur5..&c...,

Total WAURINGTON V. EGRESTONT.—Warrington were engaged at home on Saturday in giving a helping hand to a sectind- class club—Egremont. The visitors have. been steadily improving of late, and one match was darn them. The home team won the toss, but, owing to the late arrival of the visitors, it was three o'clock before a start was made. Crosfield and Tinsley commenced, to the bowling of J Walmsley and Clarke. A separation was soon effected, J J Crosfield being out to a carCh at wicket. Clarke jeined Tinsley, but was beaten at 42 by a good ball from Wai ms- ley. Tinsley and llettesworth did not stay much longer, and tbe visitors' hopes were raised when the board showed I 4 for 57. Denton and Carpenter now got together, and the I bowling, never very strong, was completely collared. Fours came quickly, especially from Carpenter. although the boundaries era very large. At 133 Denton was caught, and with Smith in another long partnership commenced. Car- penter kept hitting away, while Smith for a time WAS con- tent with singles, but finding the bowling changes were of no effect he hit out also, and runs came at a great pace. et 233 Smith (43) aud Carpenter (94) were both out, and Faircleogh and Woodhead then treated the visitors to some short rune. Kirkham made nine afterwards, leaving Podrnore not out for a similar num- ber. The innings thus closed for 265 at twenty minutes to six. TEIE WARRINGTON INTERCEPTING DEPOTS. _

Sir,—ln reading the proceeding,t of our Town Coencit on Tuesday evening last, I am glad to find that I am not alone . in making a compleint against the intercepting depot. ; Mr. Councillor Platt has donelood service to the inhabit- ' ants where these abominable places are situated in pressing the subject of the nuisances before the proper quarter, and I , trust the inhabitants and property owners will come forward . and help him. Since my last complaint of the Howley Depet, the stench from this place has been unbearable, and is extending itself along Church-street and other places, the people hitherto not knowing where the smell came from. The private complaints in this neighbourhood of Howley are universal, ad because the Medical Officer of Health and the Chairman of the Senitary Committee do not hear t'lese complaints, they coesole themselves that all is working well. It is astonishiog what fever heat is, displayed by our sanitary officials in pouncing upon a private individual who is guilty of permitting a nuisance which can scarcely bo perceivable, and upon a householder for allowing four in a bed, of ten in a house where there should only be six, and so on. for fear of an epidemic arising ; and yet gigantic nuisenees like these, in the heart of the residences of the working classes, and which are undermining the health of hundreds of the people, are allowed to continue. Aye, and gentlemen are brought in carriages to see these grand achievements, but prevesded from experiencing the smell. 'I hope when the Chairinan of the Sanitary Committee in- vita these gentlemen to a banquet again at the town's ex- pense he will choose certain due for it, and pitch the tent near one of these depots, so that these worthy gentlemen may have the advantage of the sweet smelling savour to help their appetites, as the inhabitants continu- ally have to out up with. But, Mr. Fnitor, the seriousnese of this matter lies in the fact that when one speaks to any member of the Sanitary Committee about it they are almost speechless. They refer one at once to Mr. Alderman Bureess, and tell us it is his scheme and they don't understand it; and however we com- plain the latter gentleman will stick like ghee to the, report of the Medical Officer of Health. I know full well that this gentleman has reported there is little or no nuisance to complain of, a statement which astonished me. lam quite I sure Dr. (Raman is a gentleman who, if unshackled, will do his duty; but I do think in Denning that report he Was actuated with a desire to go out of his way to compliment the chairman of the Sanitary Committee. I say at once that I am at issue with Dr. Gornalt if he persists in retying that these depots arWkot a nuisance, and it be still says re, the other medical men in the borough should be asked to give their opinion on the subject ;. that is if medical men are to be the judges. But surely others besides medical men can tell when there is an unbearable and injurious stink. The time use come when the old saving—" These I depots are there and we must make the best of them "should be diapenaed with, and if it can be proved that they exist on sufferance, and at great risk to the health of the inhabitants generally, they ought to be closed, regardless of what they j may have cost, and at the risk of offending and losing the ! valuable services ef the chairman of the Sanitary Committee —Yours truly,

div.head: WIT AND HUMOUR.
div.p: WIT AND HUMOUR.

The policeman should watch that others may not prey. Why are lovers like armies ?—BeCaUse they get along well enough until the engagement begifas. When is sugar like a'pig's tooth ?—When it's in a hogs- head." ' Although not talkative at all, the oyster is a very pleasant companion at dinner. At a recent fire, someone sent a telegram to the owner, who was away, saying, " Premises on fire; what shall we do?" The answer came prompt: "Put it out!" A disgusted young lady writes to ask if a man always acts like a fool because he is in love. No ;he does it sometimes bee fuse he is one. Lady, to servant, whom she is about to engage: "These are my conditions; do they suit you?" Servant: "H'm! I'll see. I always take ladies on trial." "Fellow slaves," began an orator at a labour meeting; and then he stopped. Go ahead!" cried a voice in the audience. "Most of us are married." When a man thinks he has a great head he allows his hair to grow long; when a woman imagines she has a mission to perform in life she cuts hers off short. A scientist now declares that the tip of the nose is the home of the soul. It has certainly often shown where , departed spirits have gone. A woman thought she had struck the concentrated essence of spitefulueis when she told her neighbour: "If you didn't wear a wig I'd like to pull your hair for you, you nasty thing."' WELLINGTON SCYBPRISED.-A young IMF once asked the Duke of Wellington point-blank in society whether he had been surprised at Waterloo. "Certainly not," said the duke;' "but lam now!" -' How are you, Smith? How are all the girls your way ? Are you as sweet on that Miss Jones as you used to be ? " Oh, no! I've left that off some time.' "Had a quarrel? " "No. Married her last month.". .

A Mr. Snaart was recently prosecuted hy a young lady for breach of promise. He settled the 'difficulty by marrying her. He made her Smart, lest she should make him smart. It is said that/Manchester has the politest lawyer in the country. A long and terrific roll of thunder having stopped him in the midst of his address to the jury, on resuming he bowed and courteously said: "Gentlemen, please excuse this interruption." A Judge, delivering a charge to a jury, said :—" Gen- tlemen, you have heard the evidence. The indictment says the prisoner was arrested for stealing a pig. This offence seems to be becoming a common one. The time has come when it must be put a stop to, otherwise, gen- tlemen, none of you will be safe." A FAIR INFERENCE.—" Pat, you've been drinkin' again." "Beggin' yer pardon, but I've not, sor." " Pshaw ! Your breath convicts you. What would you think if you should come into my room here and be greeted with un- mistakable evidences of the fumes of whisky?" " O'id thiuk, sor, it'd be mighty indecent of ye not to be lavin' the decanther where a gintleman cod hilp 'imsilf."

ETIQUETTE AS SHE IS TAUGHT AT YALE.—Before intro- ducing a gentleman to a lady, get her permission. If you can't get it, make up some plausible lie to tell the gentleman. It is impertinent to question a servant about family matters when visiting. Get hold of one of your host's children and pump him. NEITHER ONE MEANT ANy'rumo.—Jocular passenger to matter-of-fact conductor: Knocking down much to-day ?" The conductor modestly' but firmly, knocks him down. "Say.!" picking himself up, a sadder and a sorer man, "cant you taken joke? I didn't mean any- thing." "I didn't either." Time WAS NO NEED TO Scom—An old gentleman in Baltimore who used to be troubled by young men sitting up with his daughters until a late hour, settled the callers by appearing promptly at eleven o'clock and giving each of them a ticket to a ten-cent lodging-house. He never scolded or acted in an emphatic Inanner, because there wasn't any need of it. One of the cruellest remarks made by a musical au- ditor is reported from California. A vocalist was warb- ling, to her own great satisfaction, "Oh, would I were a bird ' when a rough miner shouted out, "Oh, would I were a gun." EASE BEFORE GRANDEUR.—Two housemaids out for a holiday pause 1 to look at two chandeliers in a shop win- dow—a fine eighteen branch one and one of three branches. "Which do you like best?" asked the younger maid. "The three branches,' said the elder, it's easier cleaned." "What are you waiting for, little boy?" inquired a kindly old gentleman of a street urchin who was watch- ing each passer-by intently. " Waitin' for a gent with a big moustache smokin' a cigar. Then I'll follow him and get the stub." "Do men with big mustaches smoke better cigars ?" " Nam ; but they don't smoke them so short."

"Yes," said Mrs. de Hobson, "Clara had an excellent opportunity to visit Europe last year in company with some friends; but I couldn't bear the idea of having the ocean between us." "It seems a pity, Mrs. Hobson," responded the caller. " A European trip does give such a tone to a society young lady. know it does; to those moving in the high circles that we do it is almost a necessity. I s'pose," concluded Mrs. de Hobson, half regretfully, "that I should have let he went." IN THE INTERIM.—" You are doing nicely," said the doctor encouragingly to an old darky patient..." I will call again to-morrow, and will leave you this prescrip- tion now to save you from pain in the interim. Then he went out. "Da's er 'scription dat de doctah ler," said the patient feebly to his wife, "an' I wan's yo to go to de drug sto' an' it it filled. Tell de drug sto' man dat it's fo' my interim, an' be sho an' ax him ef Ise ter take it eternally, or jess rub it on de outside, an' ef so, whar."

' -110:w. THE PRODIGAL CAME TO HIMSELF.—A certain Wesleyan minister was preaching a sermon on.the pro- digal son. He took as his text, • And when he came to himself." "We have here, brethren," said he, "an instance of the wonderful depth of meaning there is in Scripture. We see how low this unprincipled young individual had fallen. 'When he came to himself'— what does it mean? Well, look at home. What do we do when our money's gone, and we've no credit? What do we turn to? The pawnshop. So did he. First his coat would go. He might live a week on that. Then his waistcoat. That wouldn't serve him long. Lastly, his shirt would follow; and then—ah, then, my friends, he came to himself He couldn't pawn himself, and so he went home to his father."

KENTUCKY KAILROATENG.—"Do you use the block system on this road ?" inquired a passenger in a train in Kentucky. "No, sir," replied the conductor; "we have no use for it." "Do you see the electric or pneumatic signals r "No, sir." "Have you a double track 2" "No." "Wen, of course you have a train-despatcher, and runs all trains by telegraph ?" "No." "I see I,ou have no brakesman. How do you flag the rear of your train if you are stopped from any cause between stations ?" "We don't flag." • "Great heavens! What a way to run a railroad! A man takes his life in his hands when he rides on it. This is criminally reckless !" "See here, mister—if you don't like this railroad you can Fet off and walk. lam the president of this road and its sole owner. lam also the board of directors, trea- surer, secretary, general manager, superintendent, pay- master, track-master, general passenger-agent, general freight-agent, master-mechanic, ticket-agent, conductor, brakesman, and, boss. This is the Great Western Rail- road of Kentucky, six miles long, with termini at Har- rodsburg and Harrodsburg Junction. This is the only train on the road of any kind, and ahead of us is the only engine. We never have collisions. The engineer does his own firing, and runs the repair-shop and round- house all by himself. He and I run this here railway. It keeps us pretty busy; but 'we've always got time to stop and eject a sassy passenger. Do you want to ibe- have yourself and go through with us, or will you have your baggage set off here by the haystack ?" A BISHOP'S Humoun.—The Church of England Temper- ance Chronicle says :—The late Bishop of Sodor and Man was of a most genial disposition, and many examples might be given of his bright and witty sayings. A cor- respondent once wrote direct to his lordship to inquire the real meaning of the word " Sodor " as part of the bishop's title. He replied:—

What does the title "Sodor " mean? Pray tell me if you can, So strange are many facts we glean About the Isle of Man. That all the cAts are wanting tails We hear for ever more; It max be this accounts for tales Which reach the British shore. Well, " Sodorenses "—Southern Isles— Is what the title means; Although perhaps you say with smiles, "Tell that to the Marines!" For in the palmy days of old, I When things went harum-scarum - The Bishop did the title hold Of Man et Insularum." It is of the late bishop, too, of whom this anecdote is told. Upon taking his seat in a railway carriage one day, leaving his luggage in charge of the porters, one of them followed the bishop, and, politely touching his hat, put the question, "How many articles, my lord?" "Thirty- nine," said the bishop promptly, with a merry twinkle in his eye.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON. THURSDAY. Since I wrote last week the Government have passed a very bad quaner of a month. The Liberal triumph at Spalding was a serious blow, which has already had further-reaching effect thap the trans- ference of two votes on a division. It as inspiri- ted the Liberal party and has terribly frightened the Tories and their strangely-associated allies. Of course, we have heard the old argument about a bye-election signifying nothing, and the case of Southwkrk has been trotted, out once more. But there are circumstances in connection with the Spalding election which go to the root of the stand- ing controversy. It was a fair stand-up fight be- tween Liberals and the combined forces of Tories and Dissentient Liberals Lord Hartington himself had descended into the arena, and urged the elec- tors to give their votes to the Tory candidate. The result was unexpected on both sides. The most sanguine hope in Liberal quarters was that the Con- servative majority would be reduced, whilst the , Conservatives, as they had good reason to do, being ; secure of the Dissentient Liberal vote, confidently counted upon retaining the seat. The splendid and unexpected victory has sent a thrill of animation I through the Liberal ranks, which is worth fifty votes on a division. One of its effects is seen in the fight now. being made in North Paddington. Cir- cumstanees here were unusually depressing. In any case it is an uphill fight for Liberal candidates in a metropolitan constituency. But in North Paddington the candidate first chosen had at a critical moment suddenly turned tail, and the party were left in the lurch. This happened just on the eve of the Spalding election, and there is little doubt that had the result in Lincolnshire been different the North Paddington Liberals would have . accepted the situation in which they were placed, and left the Tory candidate to walk over. Thanks to Spalding they have wonderfully rallied and will at least make a stout fight. The Spalding electors gave the Government a heavy blow which has been followed up by another staggerer, dealt with suicidal hand. The Cass case is one of those forces comparatively trivial in them- 'selves, which do more to shake a Government than misfortunes in matters of high policy. It is akin to the performances of Mr. Ayrton and Mr. Lowe, which in their times did so much to shake Mr. . Gladstone's power. It is one of those blunders which is the more unpardonable because it might so easily have been avoided. But Mr. Matthews blundered from the very first. He began by curtly refusing inquiry when asked for by a Liberal mem- , her. Then, when Mr. Chamberlain interposed, he obsequiously changed his tone, and promised in- quiry. Then he withdrew his promise, and all through the debate on Tuesday night displayed a mixture of vacillation and stubbornness which was simply amazing. Had Mr. Disraeli been on the Treasury Bench, he would quickly, and promptly have _thrown over his colleague and saved the Government from obloquy. But poor Mr. Smith, though he seemed to see the error Mr. Matthews was making, had not the readiness or the courage effectually to interpose. The incident has brought sharply under public notice that curious incompe- tence of ministers which is hourly patent to any- one who observes their conduct in the House. Mr. Labouchere has gone to the root of the isiAtter in his quaint notice of motion to reduce the salary of the First Lord of the Treasury to the scale of wages of an ordinary labourer, for, as Mr. Labouchere says, any intelligent labourer could do Mr. Smith's work as well as it is accomplished by the right hon. gentle- man. The rooted conviction in the mind of tie public that the Queen really would in some material form testify to her gratitude for prolonged life and pros- perity finally took a curious form. There have not been lacking suggestions of various ways in which her Majesty might show her liberality. Nothing having come of these, some ingenious person evolved out of his (or more probably her) inner conscious- ness the idea that the Queen would make a money present, and bestow a commemorative medal upon every child born en Jubilee Day! This story, pass- ing from house to house in the back streets of towns, was greeted with amazing credulity: It is said that in some cases where the happy event came off on Jubilee Day a considerable proportion of the expected largesse was expended in entertaining friends who crowded in to congratulate the parents. However that be, it is semi-officially stated that up- wards ot 400 letters have been received by the Queen's Secretary communicating the fact of a Jubilee birth, and carefully setting forth the address of the parents, so that the gratuity and the medal might not miscarry. Of course there was nothing in the story, but its utter groundlessness has not ' lessened the disappointment in many a humble home. Although the Queen is carefully hedged about with the divinity that, as far as possible, keeps from her ears unpleasant remarks and reports; there is no . doubt she must have learned eomething of the popu- lar feeling on this subject. Indeed, it is said that her Majesty has graciously announced her intention of gratifying to the full the expectation formed. She regards in the light of a private possession the £70,000 that have been subscribed as the Women's ' Jubilee Offering. After deducting the expenses of the statue of Prince Consort, the Queen will not, it is triumphantly said, put the balance in her private purse or add it to her investments, but will dis- tribute it amongst various public charities. That, it is thought in Court circles, is &generous act that should meet to the fullest degree the general expec- tation that of all people the Queen would "come out handsome" in Jubilee time. Mr. Caine is about to take a very judicious step. Early in August he will leave England for a joiirney round the world, going by the Northern Pacific to Japan, and home through India. This is a step upon

which he is to be congratulated. It will relieve him from many embarrassments. The scene last Satur- day, where Mr. Caine was literally hooted out from I the meeting of the United Kingdom Alliance, of which he was at one time one of the most popular leaders, is indicative of the feeling which ms poli- tical conduct has excited. Lord Hartington and Mr. ' Chamberlain, wiser in their generation, are careful not to expose themselves to the criticism of a free meeting. Whenever they appear on a public plat- form, care is taken that the body of the hall shall be filled with Conservatives, and whatever sprinkling of Dissentient Liberals may be gathered by scouring the country through as wide an area as is convenient for railway journeys. Mr. iaine, strong in his old position. quite apart from politics, with temperance people, boldly turned up at Saturday's meeting, and was glad, after an ineffectual struggle, to beat an ignominous retreat. This country is evidently get- ting too hot for him, and he does wisely and well in getting out of it for a period. There has been a good deal written upon the fact that the reve'nue returns for the last qua:rter, just published, show a falling off of £200,000 in the Customs receipts. One of the morning papers sug- gests that this may be accounted for by the dimin- ished payments on account of tobacco. consequent on the unsettled state of the trade during the last three months. I had the opportunity of asking a high official in the Custom House what he thought of this suggestion, and he gave me some facts which tend to show that it is well founded. In the Victoria Docks, the principal depot of the tobacco trade in London, about three millions sterling is taken annually as duty on tobacco. In the last quar- ter there was a falling off of no less than .£BO,OOO in the duty received at these docks. Including cigars and snuff, about £9,000,000 is paid throughout the country as duty on tobacco. It is reasonable to assume that the clearances ot tobacco have fallen off in proportion with the diminution noted at the Victoria Docks. in which case it will be seen that the missing £200,000 is fully accounted for on this item alone. Notice has occasionally been taken by City editors of the London dailies of the large purchases made on Irish account of shares in Guiness's Com- pany. It appeared on the face of it that this being , an Irish industry it natually found favour in the eyes of Irish investors. But a stockbroker tells me that exceptional purchases on Irish account are not confined to the brewery companies. Irishmen,:and women too, are now, and have been since the early spring, the best customers on the London Stock Ex- change. The are apparently clearing out all their available money in Ireland, and are placing it in English securities. This is a curious and signifi- cant fact, which no doubt has its origin in the pclitical outlook. The people of Ireland who have money for investment are, of course, the landlord class, who are convinced that, in spite of political coalitions and strange alliances, Home Rule is cer- tain of accomplishment at no distant date. They are honestly convinced that Ireland. which has for centuries led a strangled existence under landlord domination, will go to the dogs under Home Rule, and they are prudently transferring their goods to another ship before the catastrophe comes.

What the bears have in their favour is the crushed state of spectilation in New York, which has been the chief leader in the rise. Brokers and operators in timerican. if their collateral securities are doubtful, are still undergoing squeezes or pressure by bank* which are winnowing out the rubbieh, And the effect is to bring about a pressure of sales here also for the time.
