This company readers of this journal were cantle.- ed against at the time of the issue of the prospectus. and it was only on the long estab- lished repute of the firm that subscriptions were forthcom- ing.

This bill came before the select committee of the House of Lords on Friday, presided over by Lord Kimberley.—The Chairman hoped the inquiry would be confined to the financial changes which had been made.—Mr. Pember, who represented the promoters, said it might be necessary to ask if their opponents had any locus standi.—The Chairman said the com- mittee had talked the matter over, and their im- pression was that they had a locus standi.—Mr. Pember in that case would not press the point. The learned counsel alien opened the case in detail, dealing only with the financial arrangements. He gave statistics of assets and expenditure, all of which -was given before the House of Commons Committee. There was another point which did not come out before the House of Commons. His friend Mr. Pope had expressed himself astonished at the smallness of the cost of raising the £4,000,000 of preference capital. He referred to the manner in which Mr. Walker had become contractor for the works, and mentioning there was a practice of underwriting shares, when arrangements were made for raising the preference Capital. It was found the company's 1 per cent would not • cover. The company would not give more, but, at this juncturevthe contractor, who was an enor- mously wealthy man, stepped in and said to the brokers he would personally insure the under- writers' commission of 31 per cent out of his own profits, in addition to the company's 14 per cent paid to Messrs Rothschild if the thing were done. Mr. Pember, in conclusion, hoped their lordships would confine•their attention to the fact whether there was any harm in the way the capital was raised.— Sir Joseph Lee then gave evidence, bearing out counsel's statement. These works included everything neces- sary to complete the canal with the exception of dredgers.—Mr Pope said he would' address himself to the question of how far their lordships were asked to interfere with section 38, which was the financial section of the bill. The object of Parlia- ment in 'inserting section 38 was to secure that this undertaking should not be carried out except in the hands of solvent people, who could .bona fide com- mand the issue of shares without a contractor's assiStance. Their lordships must decide whether, under the circumstances, this issue, sweetened as it was by Mr Walker, was. such an issue as to satisfy section 38.—Mr Bidder, Q.C., followed on behalf of the Mersey Dock Board. He contended that the capital powers of the company had been reduced, and really left no margin as security.—The room was then cleared, and after about five minutes' deliberation the Committee found the preamble proved.

Mr. Chamberlain agreed that cer- tain of the provisions of the bill needed amendment, but be thought the best CAWS,/ would be to appoint a small Mil- -1 mitten to go through the clauses in detail with a view to ' patting before the Government in regular form the views of ' the Unionist party. Mr. Finlay and other members having addressed the meeting, it was decided that Lord Hartington, Mr. Chamberlain, t.ir Henry James, Mr. Finley, Mr. T. W. Russell, Ms. Lea. div.head: EARLF.STOWN CFIURCH SCHOOL DISPUTE. THE JUDGE'S DECISION. _
div.p: THE EARLF.STOWN CFIURCH SCHOOL DISPUTE. THE JUDGE'S DECISION. _

His Honour Judge Ffoulkes, sitting at the War- rington County Court, on Thursday afternoon, gave his decision in this case, which has created con- siderable public interest. It was first beforeNtbe court on a recent sitting, when, after hearing legal arguments, his Honour reserved his decision. The case was one in which Richard Moon and others, as trustees of a certain school under a deed executed by the late Mr. William John Legh, of Lyme Park, in the county of Chester, in September, ,1857, sued the Rev. T. R. Matthews, vicar of St. John's, Earles- town, for a complete account, as treasurer, of the receipts and expenditure of the school in question for the year ending May, 1886. At the original hearing of the case, Mr. Mullholland, barrister, was for the plaintiffs, and Mr. Swift, barrister, appeared for the defendant. Mr. Mullholland, in opening the case, read extracts from the deed, showing how the funds of the school were to be managed by the principal officiating minister for the time being, and a committee, of which the licensed curate or curates and the chairman for the time being. of the Longhand North-Western Railway-the principal plaintiff in this case—were to be members. The members of the committee were to contribute a subscription of 20s tiyear each. At the time of the execution of the deed in question an ecclesiastical district was forrhed out of the parish of Newton-in- Makerfield. and the rector of the parish, the Rev. John Whitley, ceased to have anything to do with the provisions of the deed, and the Rev. Thomas Matthews, he being the incumbent of the new ec- clesiastical district, then came in. For some years subsequently the committee seemed to have fallen into abeyance, and at the beginning of 1885 it commenced to act, and held various meetings, the minutes of which counsel referred to at some length. It was owing to a difference that arose between the committee and Mr. Matthews that the present proceedings were brought. Mr. Matthews had declined to render any proper ac- count or to hand over the books and papers to the committee of the trust, and, in fact, he had put the committee at arm's length. Mr. Mulholland claimed that the committee were entitled, at the hands of the court, to obtain an account from Mr. Matthews, at all events for the year in which they had been acting. On the 14th of June a Meeting was held, and it was resolved that Dr. Harulyside be appoin- ted secretary and treasurer, which was, in fact, the removal of Mr. Matthews from that position. Vari- ous efforts were afterwards made to obtain a satis- factory statement of accounts; but Mr. Matthews declined to produce any account further than an abstract balance sheet, which was not considered satisfactory. The committee then instituted legal proceedings to gain the information they desired. Mr. Swift submitted a number of preliminary objections. First, he contended that the matter was not one which came within the jurisdiction of the court. It was not an action or suit for the execution of a trust,and merely asked the court to take an account, which, he sub- mitted, it was not within the jurisdiction of the court to do. It was also stated on the face of the claim that the trust estate did not exceed £5OO in amount or value, but he argued that it was really worth £l,BOO, and jurisdiction was only given to

the court in cases where the trust estate oa fund should not exceed .Z. 500. He also objected that the plaintiffs, as members of a committee, were not en- titled to sue a co-member and consequently a co- plaintiff. Another objection was that the action could not be maintained without the flat of the Attorney General. In giving his judgment on Thursday, his Honour said that one of the objections raised by Mr Swift was that the action could not be maintained without the fiat of the Attorney General. He hardly thought, looking at what was stated in Chancery practise, that it was a case in which the fist of the Attorney General would be required. Another objection raised was that one trustee could riot sae another, and on that Mr Swift quoted a case. He (his Honour) scarcely thought that case was strictly an authority to go upon. ' The Case referred to arose out of the sub=crip- Cons given toward& a church,,and there was Fi self-con- stituted body acting on behalf of the general holy of sub scribers, which was dwelt upon a great deal by Mr Justice Pearson. The inference to be drawn was that if they were trustees the judge was not prepared to say that where there were funris in the hands of one truistee, the other trustees might tike proceedings against him. ;He (his Honour) thoug it that there was no doubt that one trustee could sue another, and whether they could do depended upon the cir- cumstances. It was wise for trustees, before so doing, to take the a +vice of the Court of Mowery. There were many cases in which he thought trustees could take proceedings against their co-trustees,. for there were cases in which a trustee had • its hind a definite sem of money, whieh 'should be in the possession of the whole body, who, after using every exertion to get it, could not, and then took proceedings against him. Those were very different circumstances from the circumstances of the c tee now in question. The evidence regarding it did not show that defendant had anything in hand, or that he had collected anything. There was a suggestion that there were certain subscriptions that would increase the whole amount, but thilre was no direct evidence of anything being held by defendant, and therefore the circumstances were not the same as in the cases he had referred to. Another point was that the court bad 'no jurisdiction to entulain an action for an account.. In the view that he took of the law he did not think- that court had power to order an account simply. An account might be ordered where it arose incidental to other proceedings bat the court could not entertain an original action, the Obj.ct. of which was simply to render an account. He did not think he had jurisdiction to entertain an action of that kind. The action came before the court as " for an account," that was what the particulars said. If the school was a charity within the Charitable Trains Act it was possible that he should have jurisdiction to order each an account, because the Act was very wide in its language. He had already said tnat he did not think the school sego-a charity within the meaning of the Act, and he thought that Mr. Mulholland did not dissent much I' rem that opinion. The school was not en- dowed, there was simply a site given for the foundation, and therefore he could not entertain the application under tke Charitable Trusts Act: The only way in which he could entertain the action at all was under a jurisdiction Act passed in 1865) which gave the court certstin jurisdic- tion in certain specific cases, Mr. Mulholland had said that practically the case was for the execution of a trust, and he would apply for an amendment to bring it within the terrine of the Act he (his Honour)had•referred to. An amendment might be made during or after a bearing, in accordance with the evidence that was given in the case. Did the evidence in this case disclose that the action was for the exe- cution of a trust ? It might be in some senses, no doubt, but in order, be thought, to establish an action in this way it most be shown that there was some fund to be recovered, and that was where in this case he thought the evidence failed. It would be no good to amend the plaint unless the evidence would support it in. its amended form. All that the evidence showed wee that the account furnished by the defenda • t was incorrect. How mach so, or how little, it did not show. Therefore he must treat it as an action for an account, and if it was an action for an account he had no jurisdiction. Assuming for a moment that he had power to entertain it, then came the next objection—that the trust exceeded in value £5OOl After referring to the conditions in the deeds, his Honour said that it was contended that the application only included subscriptions given to the schools in the year 1886.13, and that the trust was less than t£soo. But he* could the subscriptions, given la that year be separated from the- rest of the trust estate? The committee had the control of all. There was no part of the trust that the committee had the management of to the exclusion of the other part. The trust was all one, and the committee had the management of the whole. The evidence given strongly impressed bim with, the opinion that even apart from the subscriptions the itched buildings, An, were themselves worth more than £5OO. He supposed that it would not be contended that they could split up an estate into a number of items each less than £5OO, and then bring them before the court to give jurisdiction, for in that way an estate of any kind might. be broken up, and the,Act of Parliament would be entirely evaded. He thought that this trust estate did exceed £5OO, and assuming that the action could be maintained as one of execution of trust he thought that tne wine of the estst, exceeded the amount to which jurisdiction was given to that court. Therefore he must decide that the case should be struck out as the court had net jurisdiction. Costs would follow.

div.head: RUNCORN COUNTY COURT:
div.p: RUNCORN COUNTY COURT:

TUESDAY.—Befora His Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes. Tun Catsu LIST comprised 152 original plaints, two ad- journed plaints. and =lodgment Stirrinionses. A JUDGMENT Stanton&—George Taylor, of the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, Liverpool, formerly of Runcorn, failed to appear to answer a judgment summons asking hire to show cause why he should not be committed to gaol for the non-payrnent of an account' owing to Mr. Aaron, of Weston. Mr. A. Linaker appeared for the plaintiff, and sad the defendant had forwarded a letter in which he offered to pay 10e per month, and enclosing a postal order for that amount. His Honour, after perusing the letter in which the defendant stated his salary was £125 a year, said he thought lOs a month was as much as the defendant could pay, and he made an order for that amount. A. CURIOUS AcTrow.—The Standard Mineral Water Co. 23, Seel-street, Liverpool, brought an action against Messrs. P. Smith and Co., chemists, Bridge-street, Runcorn. to re- cover £l3 15s 104 for goods supplied.—Mr. Aurelius Aubrey Devere Beauclerc, a clerk appeared for the company, and Mr. Smith appeared for the defenclants.—Mr. Smith asked if the company had not been to liquidation, and Mr. Beauclerc replied in the affirmative, but said that the business had been bought by Mr. Gilchrist, who traded under the name of company.—Mr. Smith said he was a considerable shareholder in the company, and he had had no notice of any such transaction, nor bad he received a balance sheet.— Mr.Beauclero wished to hand to his Honour a circular which he said bad been forwarded La each customer.— His Honour said the circular would not help him. It is required by law that notice in writing of the assignment of the debts should be given In order that the debtor may object to the assignment and prefer to be cued by the original creditor. He could not entertain this action in the present state of the case.—Mr. Bean- niers said Mr. Smith bad paid the amount he contended was due for liquid, into Court —His honour: That amount the Mineral Water Company will be entitled to take out, but you are not the Company; von are another person al- together. If it had not been for the questions of the de- fendant nothing would have been known of it.—Mr. Smith asked for his expenses. He should have been in Worces- ter that day, and he had been detained by that case.—His Honour adjourned the case until next court, the plaintiff to see what his rights were in the meantime. He reserved the question of costs.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tneadav afternoon. There were present Messrs Mclntyre (presiding), Hadfield, Knowles, Aaron. Grice, Lewis, Brandreth, Turner, Hamilton, Taylor Stokes, and the Rev. J. Lockwood; and Mr. H. Linaker (Clerk). Itmetrann Os' TRAWL—In answer to a question, the Workhouse Master (Mr. Cunnab) said there had recently been an increase in the number of vagrants relieved. Some of them had come into the neighbourhood to get employ- ment at the Liverpool Corporation works at Norton' and others, because they expected the Manchester Ship Canal to start.—Mr.Grioe : What at Dutton P—The Workhouse Master: Somewhere in the neighbourhood. (Laughter.) THB BOARD AND FTS COLLECTOR —The Rev. J. Lockwood said he had a matter of very grave importance to bring before them, and which had been hanging fire so long. It was nearly two years since be made a motion to the effect that their collector (Mr. Houghton) should be requested to bring his books and give a them-a statement of his accounts from time to time. Again, at aWieeting held on the 9th November, 1886, he moved that the collector draw ma a statement shewing the list of persons in *rears, and the amount owing by them. Matters went on quietly till the 24th May last, when he (Mr. Lock- wood) moved that the collector's attention, be drawn to the resolution of the 9th November, and to that the collector replied that owing to illness for some months past be had not been able to produee the statement asked for, but would do so at the next meeting. At the next meeting of the Committee, however, the collector was not present, but as the meeting was held in Jubilee week they did not think much of it, but the clerk was asked to write to the collector asking him to be at the meeting that day with his booke. A special meeting of the committee had been held at twelve o'clock that day, and seine of the members had attended at grea4inconvenienoe, but they had no collector, no books, and no statement, and they had had no communication from the collector as re- garded the matter. The committee now asked the Board , for advice as to what they should do. The collector had had every opportunity afforded him for presenting a state- ment of accounts, and the least he could have done In reply to the clerk would. have been to acknowledge the letter. Their relieving officer had met the collector the preltious night at Runcorn, and told him he would certainly be ex- pected at the meeting that day.—The Chairman said it was a very important question; it was treating the committee with utter contempt —Mr Hadfield said that independent ef treating the committee in a very improper manner, they ouaht to have a list of those paying money which was due inßuncern. The collector seemed to be treating both the com- tnittee and the Board in a very improper and cavalier man- ner, and some action should be taken in the matter.—NEr. ' Aaron said there were many children in that workhouse whose fathdrs were strong able-bodied men, and yet the Board did not know whether or not there was 6cl a week paid towards the keep of the children. It was time a change was made.—The Clerk mentioned that in one case £23 las was owing.—Me Hadfield moved that the clerk be requested
to prepare from the books a statement of what was awing. and that the collector be peremptorily requested to attend at the next meeting of the Board.—This proposal wai agreed to.
'The relief casee were thew proceeded with.
RUNCORN" SCHOOL BOARD.
The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday. Present—Messrs. S C. Beckett, E. Ellison, F. A. Lake, J. R. Frith, and G. Moss, clerk. In the absence of the chairman, Mr. Lake presided.

div.head: NEW MEMBER.
div.p: A NEW MEMBER.

_ The Clerk read the minutes of a special meeting held on the 28th June, at wtticji it was reeved by Mr Beckett and seconded by Mr Lake that the vacancy caused by the resig- nation of Mr W Handley be filled by Mr J R Frith.

div.head: SCHOOL ATTENDANCH-COMISITTSH.
div.p: SCHOOL ATTENDANCH-COMISITTSH.

During the month 62 pirents were summoned to appear before this committee to explain the irregular attendance of their chklren at school. Forty-five parents appeared, and suitable warninga were given,

div.head: THS LATE' TRBASITRIM
div.p: THS LATE' TRBASITRIM

The Clerk reported the death of Mk. B; A. Chorlton, the late treasurer to the Board.—The Chairmen proposed that the clerk be requested to write to Mrs.. Chorlton expressing the regret of the members at the death of her husband, and their sympathy with her and her family in their trouble.— Mr Imison seconded the motion, which weer unanimously passed.

div.head: TREASVICERSUIP.
div.p: THE TREASVICERSUIP.

Mr J B Holland, bank in in4ger, applied for the position of treasurer to the Board, which was made vacant through the sad death of Mr. Chorlton. Should the Board do him the honour to elect him, he should always endeavcrsr to expe- dite their business, and preserve the kindly feeling which existed between his late friend Mr ChOrlton and tberns.lves. —On the p-oposition of Mr Beckett, s.conded by Mr Frith, Mr Holland was unanimously appointed.

div.head: SCHOOL FEES QHESTION%
div.p: THE SCHOOL FEES QHESTION%

The Clerk read the following letter which he bad ad. dressed to Mr. H Linaker, clerk to the Runcorn Board of Guardiane: "Sir.—l have to inform you that your letter dated 25th nit, Waft read at the meeting of this Board held yesterday, when Mr. E. Imison disputed the accuracy of your version of the interview alluded to., It is not Imes. sary however to discuss this further,.as the Board.is willing to entertain yourauggestion that its oflacials shall deal with the applications in question. and it is theua,ht a working scheme could be best arrived at by consultation between a deputation from your Board of Guardians and our School Attendance Committee. Please let me bear from you here- on. In addition I was directed to say that this Board is exceedingly anxieue that your inqairy officer should re- sume his work pending the suggested negotiations, so that children who are now in enforced absence from school may at once commence attendance as the annual examinations will take place /Shortly. I shall be glad to bear from you that this will be done Yours truly, G. Moss, Clerk. H. Lineker, Esq., Frodsham." The reply from Mr. Linker was as follows:—" Referring to your letter of the Bth inst. as to payment of school fees in the township of Runcorn, I have to inform you that at the meeting of the Guardians held on the 23rd inst. it wee resolved that the elected Guardians for the township of Runcorn be a committee to consider applications for school fees in conjunction with a committee of your BAard."—The Clerk said the Board would observe that Mr. Linaker did not give an answer to the latter pert of his letter, in which -he said the Board wiehed that the inquiry officer should perform his duties while the negotiations were pending.— "Mr. Beckett asked what was being done with thole parents who could not afford to pay the school fees of their chil- dren? Were they not attending school, and were there many ?—The Chu* said there were a good many who were- not attending sehool.—Mr. liaison said in some instances the teachers had allowed the children to attend without fees. The teachers had taken pity on the children, and ad- mitted them —Mr. Beekett slid he knew that was so in two or three instances. It would be a pity for the schools to lose the grant, which would run from 141 61 to Yrs 61 per head for the bake of two or three shillings. Still he did not think it was right that any committee of a echool should be at the loge of that money, and some means should be taken by the Guardians in the interim by the re-anpointmentr of the inquiry officer. Let him do his duty until Buell time es the matter was settled. It would be more Satisfactory. It struck him that the Guardians did not know the position in which they stood towards this matter.—The Chairman : I don't think the Guardians appreciate the position in which the School Board was placed.—Mr. Imison said the School Board had been treated with scant courtesy by the Guardians. The proper way was to send a communication telling the Board what they wanted, and not to have suspended their , officer. They reduced the School Board to a state of abso- • lutelmpetenee straight away. That was notthe way for one public body to treat another.—On the suggestion of ttie Chairman, it was resolved that the clerk acknowledge the letter from the Guardians, and ask that the committee to he appointed should meet the School Beard Committee as early as possible.

div.head: THIS HOLIDAYS.
div.p: THIS HOLIDAYS.
It arse resolved that the schools "break up " for the holidays on the 21st inst., and re-assemble on,the 15th of August.

div.head: OUTBREAK OF MEASLES:
div.p: OUTBREAK OF MEASLES:

The Clerk reported that. measles were very prevalent in the town. The disease was of a mild nature, He noticed that on wne or two previous occasicins the schools had been fumigated or disinfected.—On the proposition of Mr. Becket it was decided that the schools should be limewashed during the holidays.

div.head: ATTENDANCES.
div.p: THE ATTENDANCES.

It was reported that during June the percentage of at- tendance at Greenwayqoad Board School was :—Mixed 60, corresoonding period last year 58-;•senior girls 85. last year 62; Mill Brew Infants, 71, last year 60. National Schools, boys 85, last year 82; girls 80, last year 81; infants 80, last year 66. Trinity Schools, bays 88; last year 88; girls 74. last year 78 ; infants 79, last year N. Wesleyan Schools. boys 86, last year 77; girls 75 last Year ; in- fants 74, last year 65. Roman Catholic School, boys, girls, and infants. 54; last year 62. Newton Infant School, 72, last year 62. The percentage of attendance of the whole of the schools was 76, last year 70; an increase of 6.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

• The monthly meeting of this body was held on Tuesday afternoon, et the new Public Offices, Victoria-square. Mr. T. S. Timmis presided, and there were also present—the Revs. J. Clarke and G. Bond, Dr. OTKeefts, and Messrs. J. W. Wareing, H. Wade Deacon, X. B. liaison, F. Heyes, and G. H. Denby (clerk).

div.head: NEW OFFICES.
div.p: THE NEW OFFICES.

Previous to commencing the business of the Board the Chairman said he thought the members might congratulate therneelves upon having removed into these commodious premises, and he consideted that their thanks were due to the Local Board for providing such excellent accommoda- tion, and to the architect for having so ably carried out his instructions. He also laoped and believed that the harmony which had characterised their proceedings through so many years in the old premises would continue to characterise their meetings in the future. (.Haar, hear.)—Dr. O'Keeffe endorsed the chairman's sentiments entirely, and hoped the arrangements proposed to be carried out by the General Purposes Committee would be satisfactory. As a member of the Local Board he had pleasure in welcoming the School Board to the new place of meeting.

div.head: SCOOT. MARAGEACEST COMMITTEE.
div.p: SCOOT. MARAGEACEST COMMITTEE.

This committee -recommended that Miss Sarah Jane I Alderson be appointed an assistant mistress in the Infants' Department of the West Bank School, at a salary of £35, 1 rising acrmrding to the scale of the Board, the engagement commencing let July, and to be terminable on either side by one month's notice. The committee also recommended that on the advice of the Medical Officer of Health the Simms Crosi and Warrington-road Schools be closed feta 1 weeks longer, from the 27th June.—Mr. Imison, in propos- ing the adoption of the minutes, said it was open for dis- cussion whethdr the:schools above mentioned should be re- opened next month.—The Chairman, in seconding, expressed the opinion that many things might happen within four weeks.—Tbe minutes were then adopted.—lt was decided that the School Management Committee be authorized to keep the Simms Cross and Warrington-mid Schools closed until they considered that the danger from the spread of measles had passed away.—During the discussion which took place Mr. Dickson (nuisance inspector), le answer to the Chairman, said it was his opinion that the epidemic was spreading. There had been about 25.deatba within a Very short period of the outbreak.—ln answer to Mr. 'Nilson, Mr. Dickson said that there was also more danger of the disease spreading when the children were at liberty than when they were at school.

div.head: TEII3 HEAMINATIONS.
div.p: TEII3 HEAMINATIONS.

The Clerk reported that the Educational Department bad consented to the drawing examination being postponed un- til November, but no reply to the request for the postpone- ment of the other examinations had been reeeived.—The Rev. J. Clarke objected to the postponement or the drawing examination, saying it would interfere with the arrange- naeute for next year.

div.head: FINANCE CODIMITTE.
div.p: FINANCE CODIMITTE.

The Finance Committee reported the following accounts had been examined by the various committees, and re• commeoded the same to be paid t—ldistrict Education Com- mittee, £29 15s; School Management Committee £355 3s; Finance Committee, £212 fie; total, 1597 9e The Committee also reported that since their last re-, port £9 es Od bad been received from hire of rooms- and £l,OOO had been/paid into the bank. They further re ported that they haraccepted the tender of Mr Sadler for removing the furniture and fittings from the old office to the new public offices, and making the alterations to the fittings and supplying new desks, 8 helve, Lc. They had also accepted the tender of Mr Miller,Waterloo-road, for lino- leum for the committee-rooms and clerk's office, and offered, subject to the approval of the Board, to Parr's Banking Company the fixtures in the old offices, consisting of speak- ing tubes, venetian blinds, ventilators, &0., for the sum of £l5.
The minutes WKS then adopted, en the motion of Dr. O'Keefe, seconded by the Chairman, and the Board rose.

The Board of Trade returns show that the imports for June decreased £4546,724, and the exports decreased £1.215,634. ' It is announced that on Wednesday next, the Queen, with other members of the Royal Family, will pay a short visit to Hatfield House, Lord Salisbury's Hertfordshire residence. _ _
